title: Leonardo da Vinci
intro: Leonardo finished very few paintings, and they are now spread across five cities. He spent his life moving between patrons in Florence, Milan, Rome, and France, often leaving work half done when something more interesting came along.
This thread follows his working life and the paintings it left behind.

chapters.heading: Apprentice
chapters.text: Leonardo trained in the workshop of Andrea del Verrocchio, a sculptor and painter who supplied Florence’s churches and guild halls. Vasari tells the story that after the young Leonardo painted an angel in Verrocchio’s Baptism of Christ, his master gave up painting.

chapters.heading: The Last Supper
chapters.text: He wrote to the Duke of Milan offering himself mainly as a military engineer, mentioning painting near the end. In Milan he painted the Last Supper on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie, in an experimental technique that started flaking within his lifetime. He also turned a hall of the Sforza castle into a forest of painted trees.

chapters.heading: Lady with an Ermine
chapters.text: In Milan he also painted Cecilia Gallerani, the duke’s teenage mistress, holding an ermine. It was bought for a Polish princess around 1800, the Nazis took it, and it came back to Kraków after the war. It is one of only four portraits of women by Leonardo.

chapters.heading: The battle with Michelangelo
chapters.text: Back in Florence, the republic hired Leonardo and the young Michelangelo to paint rival battle scenes on facing walls of the great council hall. Neither finished. Leonardo’s experimental paint ran, and Michelangelo was called away to Rome.

chapters.heading: A drawing the size of a painting
chapters.text: The Burlington House Cartoon, a full-size chalk drawing of the Virgin, Saint Anne, and the infants, was never turned into a painting. The National Gallery bought it in 1962 after a public appeal.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: He started the portrait of Lisa del Giocondo in Florence and kept working on it for years, taking it with him to France, where he died in 1519. It became the world’s most famous painting partly because it was stolen from the Louvre in 1911 and missing for two years.

image: The Last Supper Leonardo Da Vinci - High Resolution.jpg

title: Michelangelo
intro: Michelangelo thought of himself as a sculptor, but popes kept making him paint and build. He spent his working life going back and forth between Florence and Rome, and most of what he made is still in those two cities.
This thread follows him between them, plus two pieces that ended up in Paris and London.

chapters.heading: The Pietà
chapters.text: A French cardinal commissioned a marble of Mary holding the dead Christ for his tomb. Michelangelo was in his early twenties. It is the only work he ever signed, on the sash across Mary’s chest.

chapters.heading: David
chapters.text: Back in Florence, he took a tall block of marble that had been started and abandoned decades before and carved David from it. A committee that included Leonardo decided to put it outside the town hall instead of on the cathedral. It stood there until 1873, when it moved into the Accademia. A copy now stands in its place.

chapters.heading: The tomb
chapters.text: Pope Julius II called him to Rome to build a huge freestanding tomb with more than forty statues. Money and politics cut it down over forty years to a wall tomb with Moses at the center. In 1506, while he was in Rome, the Laocoön was dug up in a vineyard and he was sent to look at it.

chapters.heading: The ceiling
chapters.text: Julius then made him paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, a job he didn’t want. He worked standing on scaffolding, not lying on his back, and it took four years. Raphael was painting rooms for the same pope down the corridor.

chapters.heading: Two slaves
chapters.text: He carved two bound figures for the tomb, then they were dropped from the plan. He gave them away, and they went to France. They are now in the Louvre.
chapters.image: Dying and Rebellious Slaves by Michelangelo (Louvre).jpg

chapters.heading: The Medici rooms
chapters.text: For the Medici he designed a funeral chapel at San Lorenzo, with reclining figures of Night, Day, Dawn, and Dusk, and a library with a staircase that seems to pour into the entrance hall. In 1530, after siding with the republic against the Medici, he is thought to have hidden in a small room under the chapel. Drawings on its walls were found in 1975.
chapters.image: Tomb of Lorenzo, Duke of Urbino, New Sacristy (Medici Chapel), San Lorenzo, Florence (2) (48768615417).jpg

chapters.place: Sistine Chapel and St. Peter’s, Rome
chapters.heading: Judgment and the dome
chapters.text: He moved to Rome for good in 1534 and painted the Last Judgment on the chapel’s altar wall. In his seventies he took over the building of St. Peter’s and designed its dome, and he laid out the square on the Capitoline Hill. He died in Rome in 1564, and his body was taken to Florence to be buried.
chapters.image: Dome of St. Peter's Basilica by Michelangelo (7990081751).jpg

chapters.heading: A copy for London
chapters.text: The Grand Duke of Tuscany gave Queen Victoria a full-size plaster cast of David. It stands in the V&A’s Cast Courts with other copies of famous works. A plaster fig leaf was made for it so it could be covered for royal visits.

title: Caravaggio
intro: Michelangelo Merisi took his name from the town his family came from, east of Milan. In about fifteen years in Rome he changed how European painting handled light, and he did it while getting into court cases, sword fights and, in 1606, a killing.
He spent his last four years as a fugitive. His paintings are now spread across Europe, some still in the chapels they were made for.

chapters.place: Milan and the town of Caravaggio
chapters.heading: Training in Lombardy
chapters.text: Born in Milan in 1571 and raised partly in Caravaggio after plague killed his father. At 13 he was apprenticed to Simone Peterzano, a Milanese painter who said he had trained under Titian. Lombard painters liked plain, closely observed detail, and he took that with him. His Basket of Fruit, painted later in Rome, is in Milan’s Biblioteca Ambrosiana.

chapters.place: San Luigi dei Francesi and Santa Maria del Popolo, Rome
chapters.heading: Fame in two chapels
chapters.text: He arrived in Rome broke and painted fruit and flowers for other artists. His break was the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi in 1600: the Calling of Saint Matthew, with a shaft of light across a tax office. Two more canvases for Santa Maria del Popolo followed. Both churches are free, and the paintings are still where he hung them.
chapters.image: Paintings by Caravaggio at Contarelli Chapel-3.jpg

chapters.heading: A death on the tennis court
chapters.text: In May 1606 a fight near the tennis courts on Via della Pallacorda ended with Caravaggio killing Ranuccio Tomassoni. He was sentenced to death in absentia, which meant anyone could kill him on sight, and he left Rome.
chapters.image: Caravaggio - David with the Head of Goliath - Vienna.jpg

chapters.heading: Sanctuary in Naples
chapters.text: Naples was Spanish-ruled and outside the Pope’s reach. He was in demand at once: the Seven Works of Mercy, painted for a charity’s chapel, still hangs over its altar. The Flagellation of Christ is at Capodimonte.

chapters.place: Valletta, Syracuse, Messina, Palermo, and Porto Ercole
chapters.heading: On the run
chapters.text: In Malta he was made a Knight of the Order of St. John, then jailed after another fight, escaped, and was expelled. He moved through Sicily painting altarpieces, went back to Naples, and was badly cut in the face outside a tavern. He died in July 1610 at Porto Ercole, on his way to Rome to ask for a pardon. He was 38.

chapters.heading: Where the paintings went
chapters.text: Collectors and dukes moved his easel paintings north. The Death of the Virgin was turned down by the church that ordered it and bought for the Duke of Mantua on Rubens’s advice; it is now in the Louvre. The Taking of Christ was lost for two centuries and turned up in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin.

title: The Dutch Golden Age
intro: In the 1600s a small, newly independent republic became the richest place in Europe, and its merchants wanted pictures of themselves, their houses, and their dinners. Rembrandt, Vermeer, and Frans Hals painted for that market.
Their work has since scattered from Amsterdam to Berlin, Paris, London, Vienna, and Florence, along with a few stories about who owned it.

chapters.heading: A city of merchants
chapters.text: Amsterdam began digging its ring of canals in 1613 to house the traders who were making it rich. The tall, narrow houses along the Herengracht were built for the same people who bought paintings.
chapters.image: Gerrit Adriaensz. Berckheyde - The Bend in the Herengracht in Amsterdam - WGA1920.jpg

chapters.heading: Frans Hals
chapters.text: In Haarlem, Frans Hals painted portraits so fast you can see each brushstroke. Two of his best are in Berlin: a boy singing with a flute, and Malle Babbe, a real Haarlem woman with a tankard and an owl on her shoulder.
chapters.image: Frans Hals Malle Babbe about 1640-1646 Gemäldegalerie Berlin 9387.jpg

chapters.heading: The Night Watch
chapters.text: An Amsterdam militia company paid Rembrandt for a group portrait, and he painted them moving, half in shadow. It got its name later, when its varnish had darkened. In 1715 it was trimmed on all sides to fit a wall in the town hall.

chapters.heading: A girl at a window
chapters.text: Rembrandt’s Girl at a Window leans on a sill so convincingly that a story grew up about it being set in a real window to fool passers-by. It hangs in Dulwich Picture Gallery in south London, which opened in 1817 as England’s first public art gallery.

chapters.heading: Bathsheba
chapters.text: Rembrandt’s Bathsheba was probably modeled by Hendrickje Stoffels, who lived with him without marrying him. The year he painted it, his church summoned her for living in sin.

chapters.heading: Vermeer’s rooms
chapters.text: In Delft, Johannes Vermeer painted slowly, about 35 pictures in all, most of them one or two people in a room lit from the left. The Milkmaid is in the Rijksmuseum. The Glass of Wine, a quiet courtship by a stained-glass window, is in Berlin.

chapters.heading: Late Rembrandt
chapters.text: Rembrandt went bankrupt in 1656 and lost the house where he had made most of his etchings. His late paintings got rougher and thicker. Van Gogh said he would give ten years of his life to sit in front of The Jewish Bride with a crust of bread.

chapters.heading: The painting Vermeer kept
chapters.text: Vermeer never sold The Art of Painting, which shows a painter at work on a model dressed as the muse of history. In 1940 Hitler bought it for the museum he planned in Linz. It is now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum.

chapters.heading: Rachel Ruysch
chapters.text: The Golden Age outlived Rembrandt. Rachel Ruysch painted flowers and fruit with insects crawling over them, became court painter to a German prince, and sold her pictures for more than Rembrandt’s had fetched.

chapters.heading: The fake Vermeers
chapters.text: After the war Dutch police arrested Han van Meegeren for selling a Vermeer to Hermann Göring. To avoid a treason charge he admitted he had painted it himself, along with several other “Vermeers,” and proved it by painting another under supervision.

image: The Night Watch - Rembrandt Harmenszoon van Rijn.png

title: Van Gogh
intro: Vincent van Gogh painted for only ten years and sold almost nothing in his lifetime. Today he is one of the most famous painters in the world.

He moved often, and each move changed his work. This thread follows him from a lodging house in London to a village inn outside Paris, and ends at the Amsterdam museum that holds most of his paintings.
image: Van Gogh - Starry Night - Google Art Project.jpg

chapters.heading: A young art dealer in London
chapters.text: Before he was a painter, Van Gogh sold paintings. At twenty he was working for Goupil & Co, a large firm of art dealers, and in 1873 they sent him to their London branch near Covent Garden. He rented a room south of the river, at 87 Hackford Road in Stockwell, and walked across the Thames to work each morning. He fell in love with his landlady’s daughter, but she was already engaged and turned him down. A small drawing he made of the house survives. Unhappy and distracted, he did badly at work, and by 1876 the firm had let him go. He turned to religion instead.
chapters.tip: The house is now Van Gogh House, an artists’ residency that opens for events. A blue plaque marks it.

items: If you want more on his London years, a podcast episode asks how the city set him on the road to painting.

chapters.heading: Hours in front of a Rembrandt
chapters.text: His next plan was to become a minister. In 1877 he moved to Amsterdam to study for the university entrance exams in theology, living with an uncle who ran the city’s naval dockyard. Latin and Greek defeated him, and he gave up within a year. Amsterdam mattered to him in another way, though. He came back in 1885, soon after the new Rijksmuseum opened, and sat for hours in front of The Jewish Bride, a late painting by Rembrandt, the great Dutch painter of the 1600s. He wrote that he would give ten years of his life to sit there for two weeks with only a crust of dry bread.

items: To look more closely at The Jewish Bride, there is a podcast episode about the painting he sat in front of for hours.

chapters.place: Nuenen, and the Van Gogh Museum, Amsterdam
chapters.heading: His first big painting
chapters.text: After Amsterdam he tried preaching to coal miners in southern Belgium, and failed at that too. In 1880, at 27, he decided to become an artist. He taught himself to draw, and in 1883 he went to live with his parents in Nuenen, a village in the south of the Netherlands where his father was the pastor. There he painted the people he saw every day, weavers at their looms and families working the fields, almost always in dark browns and grays. The Potato Eaters, from 1885, was his first ambitious picture: a family eating supper by lamplight. Even his friends disliked it. It now hangs in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam.
chapters.image: The Potato Eaters - Vincent Van Gogh.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to look harder at The Potato Eaters.
items: A longer video explains what Van Gogh wanted the painting to say, and why critics disliked it.
In a shorter one, two art historians look at why he painted farm workers, and how the rough brushwork suits the family’s hard life.

chapters.heading: Paris teaches him color
chapters.text: In early 1886 he turned up in Paris without warning and moved in with his younger brother, Theo, an art dealer who had been sending him money for years. That summer they took a bigger apartment together at 54 rue Lepic, high on the hill of Montmartre. Through Theo he met painters who were trying new things, among them the Impressionist Camille Pissarro and Paul Gauguin. He also began collecting cheap Japanese woodblock prints, with their flat, bright colors. Over two years he painted about two hundred pictures, and his palette moved from muddy browns to strong reds, yellows, and blues.
chapters.image: 54 rue Lepic, Theo and Vincent Van Goghs Paris house 2010.jpg

items: For more on these two years, there is a podcast episode in which two art historians explain how Paris and the Japanese prints changed the way he painted.

chapters.heading: A yellow house in the south
chapters.text: Paris wore him out. In February 1888 he took the train south to Arles, a small town in Provence, hoping to find the light and color he had seen in the Japanese prints. He rented four rooms in a yellow house on the town’s Place Lamartine and painted quickly: orchards in blossom, the café on the square at night, and the stars over the river Rhône. He dreamed of a “studio of the south” where artists would live and work together, and he talked Gauguin into joining him. To decorate Gauguin’s room, he painted a series of sunflowers in a vase. Gauguin arrived in October. One of those sunflower paintings now hangs in the National Gallery in London.
chapters.image: Vincent van Gogh - The yellow house ('The street').jpg

mediaNote.lead: Three things here take you further into that year in Arles.
items: A podcast episode looks at Starry Night over the Rhône, his painting of the stars over the river.
A feature-length documentary follows the sunflower paintings from Arles to museums around the world.
A short video looks at the self-portrait Gauguin sent him that year.

chapters.heading: The night he cut his ear
chapters.text: The two men painted side by side for nine weeks, but they argued constantly. On the night of December 23, 1888, after a bad quarrel, Van Gogh cut off part of his left ear with a razor and gave it to a young woman who worked at a nearby brothel. Gauguin left for Paris within days. Van Gogh was treated at the town hospital, now a cultural center called the Espace Van Gogh, and a few weeks later he painted himself with his head bandaged. More breakdowns followed. In May 1889 he asked to be admitted to an asylum in Saint-Rémy, a nearby town, and it was there that he painted The Starry Night.

mediaNote.lead: There are two ways to stay with this part of the story.
items: A podcast episode takes a slow look at the self-portrait with the bandaged ear, which now hangs in the Courtauld Gallery in London.
A short video argues that his colors and compositions often reflected his state of mind.

chapters.heading: His last seventy days
chapters.text: A year later he felt well enough to leave. In May 1890 he moved to Auvers-sur-Oise, a village an hour north of Paris, where Dr. Paul Gachet, a doctor who knew many artists, had agreed to keep an eye on him. He took a small attic room at the Auberge Ravoux, an inn on the main street, and painted almost every day, about seventy pictures in seventy days. On July 27 he shot himself in the chest, probably in the fields outside the village, and walked back to the inn. Theo came from Paris, and Vincent died two days later with his brother beside him. Tree Roots, a tangle of trunks at the edge of a field, was probably the last painting he worked on.
chapters.image: Vincent van Gogh - Wheatfield with crows - Google Art Project.jpg

mediaNote.lead: If you want to know more about how it ended, there are three places to go.
items: In a podcast episode, two art historians go through his last weeks in Auvers.
A video looks at Tree Roots, and at the recent discovery of the exact spot he painted.
Loving Vincent is a feature film that investigates how he died, and every frame of it is an oil painting.

chapters.heading: Jo, who made him famous
chapters.text: Theo was already ill, and he died six months after his brother. His widow, Johanna van Gogh-Bonger, known as Jo, was left with a baby son, hundreds of Vincent’s paintings, and the hundreds of letters the brothers had written to each other. Almost nobody wanted the paintings. Jo spent the rest of her life changing that. She lent them to exhibitions, sold them carefully, and in 1914 published the letters, which made people care about the man as well as the work. Her son, also named Vincent, later put the family collection into a foundation, and the Van Gogh Museum opened in 1973 to show it.
chapters.tip: Tickets are timed and sell out; book online. The paintings are hung in the order he made them.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here carry the story on.
items: A podcast episode tells how Jo made Van Gogh famous.
Van Gogh: The Life is a long biography, built on his letters.

title: Picasso and Cubism
intro: Pablo Picasso was the most famous artist of the 20th century, and Cubism, the style he invented with his friend Georges Braque, changed how painters showed the world.

This thread follows him from art school in Barcelona to the studios of Paris, where a handful of painters took apart the old rules of picture-making. It ends in Madrid, with the painting he made about the bombing of a small Basque town.

chapters.heading: A teenager in Barcelona
chapters.text: Picasso was born in 1881 in Málaga, in the south of Spain. His father was a painting teacher, and when Pablo was 13 the family moved to Barcelona, where his father had taken a post at the city’s art school, La Llotja. The boy enrolled there too, and he quickly outgrew his teachers. By 15 he was painting large, polished pictures in the traditional style the school taught. You can see them in the Picasso Museum, which fills five medieval palaces on Carrer de Montcada in the old town. Many visitors are surprised at how conventional, and how skilled, the young Picasso was.
chapters.image: 062 Casa Finestres, Museu Picasso, c. Montcada 23 (Barcelona), pati.jpg

items: For a short tour, there is a video about the museum and the student work that shows how fast he learned.

chapters.heading: The Bateau-Lavoir
chapters.text: Barcelona was not enough for him. After several trips to Paris, he settled there in 1904, at 22, in a run-down building of studios on the hill of Montmartre. It was cold in winter and had one water tap for the whole house. His friend the poet Max Jacob nicknamed it the Bateau-Lavoir, after the laundry boats moored on the Seine. Picasso lived there for five years. He painted circus performers in soft pinks, in what is now called his Rose Period, and he met Fernande Olivier, who became his partner. The building burned in 1970 and was rebuilt, but the little square in front of it is much as he knew it.

items: If you want to see it on foot, a walking tour of Montmartre passes the Bateau-Lavoir on its way up the hill to Sacré-Cœur.

chapters.heading: Les Demoiselles d’Avignon
chapters.text: In 1907, in his Bateau-Lavoir studio, he worked for months on a large canvas of five naked women. Their bodies are made of sharp, flat angles, and two of the faces look like masks, influenced by African and ancient Iberian sculpture he had been studying. He named it after Carrer d’Avinyó, a street of brothels in Barcelona’s old town that he had known as a teenager. A friend later gave it the title it has now, Les Demoiselles d’Avignon, the young ladies of Avignon. When Picasso showed it to his friends, most of them were shocked. He kept it in the studio and did not exhibit it until 1916. It is now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.

items: For more on what makes it so strange, there is a video about how its masks and broken-up space opened the way to Cubism.

chapters.heading: Little cubes
chapters.text: One of the friends who saw the painting was Georges Braque, a young French painter. At first he hated it, and then it set him thinking. In the summer of 1908 he went to paint at L’Estaque, a fishing village on the coast just north of Marseille. Paul Cézanne, the painter both men admired most, had worked there years before. Braque reduced the houses, trees, and railway viaduct to simple blocks. When he showed the pictures in Paris that autumn, a critic said they were made of little cubes. The name Cubism stuck. For the next six years, Braque and Picasso worked so closely that their pictures can be hard to tell apart.
chapters.image: L'Estaque - Chemin de la Nerthe - Viaduc ferroviaire du Marinier.jpg

items: To see how he did it, there is a short video in which two art historians look at his painting of the viaduct, with the houses turned into simple shapes.

chapters.heading: Questioned over the Mona Lisa
chapters.text: Cubism made Picasso well known, and in 1911 he nearly became notorious. That August the Mona Lisa disappeared from the Louvre, and nobody knew who had taken it. The police soon turned to Picasso’s friend the poet Guillaume Apollinaire. A former secretary of his had earlier stolen small ancient Iberian stone heads from the museum, and had sold two of them to Picasso. Apollinaire was arrested and spent several days in jail, and Picasso was called in for questioning. Neither of them had anything to do with the Mona Lisa. It turned up two years later in Florence, taken by an Italian handyman who had worked at the Louvre.

items: If you want the whole story, there is a brisk book about the theft and how the empty wall made the painting even more famous.

chapters.place: House of the Black Madonna, Prague
chapters.heading: Cubist buildings
chapters.text: Cubism soon spread beyond Paris, and in Prague it did something it did almost nowhere else: it became architecture. Around 1910 a group of young Czech architects decided that the angles and broken surfaces of Cubist painting could be built. The best example is the House of the Black Madonna, a department store designed by Josef Gočár and finished in 1912, just off the Old Town Square. Its window frames, balconies, and even its staircase are made of crisp, slanting planes. The building is named after a small statue of the Virgin from an older house on the site, which still stands in a cage on the corner. The first floor is a café, the Grand Café Orient, with Cubist lamps and furniture.

items: To see it as part of a longer walk, an introductory tour of Prague starts outside this building and ends across the river in the Lesser Town.

chapters.heading: The first collage
chapters.text: Back in Paris, Picasso and Braque kept pushing. In 1912 Picasso glued a piece of oilcloth onto a small oval still life. The oilcloth was printed to look like the woven cane seat of a chair, and he framed the picture with a length of rope. Putting a ready-made material into a painting was new, and Still Life with Chair Caning is often called the first collage in modern art. It hangs in the Musée Picasso, in a 17th-century mansion in the Marais, the old quarter on the Right Bank. The museum opened in 1985. Most of its collection is work Picasso kept for himself, which went to the French state after his death in 1973 in place of inheritance taxes.

items: For a closer look, there is a short video about the picture and why a piece of oilcloth mattered so much.

chapters.heading: Guernica
chapters.text: The partnership with Braque ended in 1914, when Braque went to fight in the First World War. Picasso went on changing styles for another sixty years, but his most famous painting is about war. On April 26, 1937, during the Spanish Civil War, German and Italian planes supporting General Franco bombed Guernica, a small town in the Basque Country, in the north of Spain. Picasso had been asked to make a painting for the Spanish Republic’s pavilion at the World’s Fair in Paris. He painted Guernica in about five weeks, in black, white, and gray, with a bull, a screaming horse, and a mother holding her dead child. He refused to let it go to Spain while Franco ruled. It arrived in 1981, after Franco’s death, and has hung in the Reina Sofía museum in Madrid since 1992.

mediaNote.lead: There are four good ways into Guernica, from a short video to a long conversation.
items: A video from Smarthistory walks through the painting and its long road to Madrid.
Great Art Explained looks at how he made it in a few weeks, and what the bull, the horse, and the lamp might mean.
In a longer podcast episode, Melvyn Bragg and his guests discuss both the bombing and the painting.
And a short episode of Witness History tells the story through the people who survived the bombing.

title: Mozart
intro: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart wrote more than six hundred works in a life of 35 years, and many of them were first heard in rooms you can still visit.

This thread follows him from a palace in Vienna, where he played as a small boy, through the opera houses of Milan, Munich, and Prague, to the Vienna apartment where he wrote The Marriage of Figaro. It ends in Seville, a city he never saw, but where two of his operas are set.

chapters.heading: Playing for the empress
chapters.text: Mozart was born in 1756 in Salzburg, a small city in the Alps ruled by its archbishop. His father, Leopold, was a violinist in the archbishop’s orchestra, and he soon saw that both his children were extraordinary. In 1762 he took them to Vienna, the capital of the Habsburg empire. At Schönbrunn, the imperial family’s summer palace on the edge of the city, six-year-old Wolfgang and his older sister, Nannerl, played for Empress Maria Theresa. A family story says the boy slipped on the polished floor and was helped up by one of the young archduchesses, Marie Antoinette. He thanked her and said he would marry her. Leopold spent much of the next ten years taking the children on tour, from London to Naples.

items: For a look inside, there is a short video tour of the palace and its state rooms.

chapters.heading: Writing down a secret
chapters.text: On the longest of those journeys, father and son spent more than a year in Italy, the home of opera. They reached Rome in Holy Week of 1770. In the Sistine Chapel, in the Vatican, the pope’s choir sang the Miserere by Gregorio Allegri, a setting of a psalm written in the 1630s. It was sung only there, only in that week, and the Vatican did not allow it to be copied. The fourteen-year-old Mozart heard it once, then wrote the whole piece out from memory that evening. He went back later in the week to check a few details. A few months later, the pope made him a knight.
chapters.image: Pope Pius VII in the Sistine Chapel A29940.jpg

items: To hear what he heard, there is a recording of the Miserere, with its high, floating line for a solo soprano.

chapters.heading: His first big opera
chapters.text: Italy gave him his first big chance in opera. Milan, then ruled by Austria, commissioned a serious opera from him for its winter season. Mitridate, re di Ponto, the story of an ancient king and his rival sons, opened on December 26, 1770. The theater was inside the Palazzo Reale, the royal palace next to the cathedral. Mozart was fourteen, and he directed it from the keyboard. Some of the singers had doubted that a boy could write for them, but the opera was a success and ran for more than twenty nights. The theater burned down in 1776, and the city built La Scala to replace it.
chapters.image: Veduta di tre quarti del Palazzo Reale di Milano.jpg

items: For a taste of the opera, there is a recording of its overture.

chapters.heading: Idomeneo
chapters.text: Back home, Mozart worked for the archbishop of Salzburg, and he hated it. The archbishop treated his musicians as servants and rarely let him travel. In 1780 the court of Bavaria, in Munich, commissioned a new opera, and he was given leave to write it. Idomeneo is about a king of Crete who makes a terrible vow to the god of the sea. It opened in January 1781 in the Cuvilliés Theatre, a small, gilded theater in the royal palace. It is his first great opera. A few months later he quarreled with the archbishop in Vienna and resigned. One of the archbishop’s officials, Count Arco, ended the argument by kicking him out of the room.

items: To hear how it begins, there is a recording of the overture.

chapters.heading: Ten years in Vienna
chapters.text: Mozart decided to stay in Vienna and live as a freelance musician, which almost nobody did at the time. He gave concerts, taught pupils, and wrote music for anyone who would pay. In 1782 he married Constanze Weber, a singer, in St. Stephen’s Cathedral. The couple moved house more than a dozen times. The grandest of their homes was an apartment on Domgasse, a narrow street behind the cathedral, where they lived from 1784 to 1787. There he wrote The Marriage of Figaro, a comic opera about servants who outwit their master, with words by the poet Lorenzo Da Ponte. It is the only one of his Vienna homes that survives, and it is now a museum called the Mozarthaus.
chapters.tip: The Mozarthaus museum keeps the Domgasse apartment’s rooms. St. Stephen’s, where he married and where his funeral service was held, is around the corner.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into his years in Vienna.
items: A podcast episode looks at “Dove sono,” an aria from The Marriage of Figaro in which the Countess remembers happier days with her husband.
A short, brisk biography shows him as a working musician, always chasing commissions and money.
And a walking tour of the old town follows him, Beethoven, and Vivaldi, with their music playing as you go.

chapters.heading: The city that loved him most
chapters.text: Figaro did well in Vienna, but in Prague, the capital of Bohemia, it was a sensation. People hummed its tunes in the streets, and Mozart traveled there to see it for himself. The city then commissioned a new opera, and he wrote Don Giovanni, again with Da Ponte, about a nobleman who seduces women and is dragged down to hell. Mozart finished it in Prague and conducted the premiere at the Estates Theatre on October 29, 1787. The story goes that he wrote the overture the night before. “My Praguers understand me,” he is supposed to have said. The theater still stands, almost unchanged, and it still stages his operas.

mediaNote.lead: Two things are worth hearing before a night at the Estates Theatre.
items: A recording of the overture opens with the dark chords that return when a statue comes to drag Don Giovanni away.
A live comedy history podcast follows his whole life, from child star to working musician, and explains why Prague loved him.

chapters.heading: An unfinished Requiem
chapters.text: His last year was one of his busiest. In 1791 he wrote The Magic Flute for a popular theater on the edge of Vienna. He also accepted a strange commission for a Requiem, a mass for the dead, from a patron who wanted to stay anonymous. That autumn he fell ill. He died on December 5, 1791, at his apartment on Rauhensteingasse, a few streets from Domgasse, with the Requiem unfinished. He was 35. The doctors called it a fever, and the real cause is still argued over. The story that he was poisoned by a rival, the composer Antonio Salieri, has no evidence behind it. His widow, Constanze, had the Requiem finished by one of his pupils so that she could be paid for it.

mediaNote.lead: His death left a mystery and an unfinished masterpiece, and there are two good ways to explore both.
items: In a long podcast episode, a conductor explains the Requiem and the mystery around it.
A video by a food historian looks at his last weeks, including the supper some people blame for his death.

chapters.heading: A city he never saw
chapters.text: Two of the operas he wrote with Da Ponte, The Marriage of Figaro and Don Giovanni, are set in Seville, in the south of Spain, a city Mozart never visited. Figaro was based on a French play by Pierre Beaumarchais, the second in a series about Figaro, a clever barber. The first play, The Barber of Seville, became an opera by Gioachino Rossini in 1816, thirty years after Mozart’s. So the prequel reached the stage after the sequel, and it became just as famous. In the old Santa Cruz quarter, guides still point out balconies said to belong to both stories.
chapters.image: Jardines de la plaza de Santa Cruz.jpg

items: If you want the prequel’s story, there is a podcast episode about The Barber of Seville and its disastrous first night.

title: Opera houses
intro: Opera started at Italian courts and became a paying public entertainment in Venice in 1637. Over the next three centuries every capital wanted its own opera house, and some of the most famous first nights were disasters.
This thread visits the houses, the premieres, and one assassination.

chapters.heading: Opera goes public
chapters.text: The first public opera house, where anyone with a ticket could get in, opened in Venice in 1637. Claudio Monteverdi, who ran the music at St. Mark’s, wrote his last operas for the city’s new theaters. He is buried in the Frari.

chapters.heading: San Carlo
chapters.text: The Bourbon king of Naples built the Teatro di San Carlo next to his palace in 1737. It is the oldest opera house still in use. In the early 1800s its manager, Domenico Barbaja, hired Rossini and then Donizetti to write for it.

chapters.heading: La Scala
chapters.text: La Scala opened in 1778 on the site of a demolished church. Verdi’s Nabucco made his name there in 1842, and Puccini’s Madama Butterfly was booed off at its first night in 1904. In the 1950s it was where Maria Callas sang her greatest roles.

chapters.heading: Shot at a masked ball
chapters.text: King Gustav III built Stockholm’s opera house and was shot at a masked ball there in March 1792. He died two weeks later. Verdi turned the story into Un ballo in maschera, though the censors made him move it to Boston.
chapters.image: Kungliga Operan Royal Swedish Opera Stockholm 2016 01.jpg

chapters.heading: An opera starts a revolution
chapters.text: On August 25, 1830, La Monnaie staged La Muette de Portici, about a Neapolitan revolt. During a duet about love of country the audience began to riot, and the unrest in the streets that night grew into the revolution that created Belgium.
chapters.image: 1004 Royal Theatre of La Monnaie in Brussels Photo by Giles Laurent.jpg

chapters.heading: Tristan in three cities
chapters.text: Wagner began Tristan und Isolde as a political exile in Zurich, where he fell for Mathilde Wesendonck. He wrote the second act in a palazzo on Venice’s Grand Canal. It was called unperformable until Ludwig II of Bavaria paid Wagner’s debts and had it staged in Munich in 1865.

chapters.heading: The Palais Garnier
chapters.text: Charles Garnier’s opera house opened in 1875 after fourteen years of building, with a grand staircase meant for being seen on. A water tank under its foundations gave Gaston Leroux the underground lake in The Phantom of the Opera.
chapters.image: Grand Staircase of Palais Garnier, Paris, France.jpg

chapters.heading: Mahler’s house
chapters.text: The Court Opera on the Ringstrasse opened in 1869. Gustav Mahler ran it from 1897 to 1907 and made it the best in Europe. It burned after bombing in March 1945, and its reopening in 1955, the year Austria regained its independence, was a national event.

chapters.heading: A roof to walk on
chapters.text: Oslo’s opera house opened in 2008 on the harbor at Bjørvika. Its sloping white marble roof rises out of the fjord, and anyone can walk up it, ticket or not.
chapters.image: Roof of the Oslo Opera House.jpg

title: Songs of longing
intro: Many European cities have a song form built on missing something: a home, a lover, a country, a self. Most grew in port districts and poor quarters, often among people who had arrived from somewhere else, and most were looked down on before they became national treasures.
This one has no timeline. Start anywhere, and listen before you read.

chapters.heading: Saudade in the old quarters
chapters.text: Fado comes out of 19th-century Lisbon: sailors’ bars, brothels, and taverns in Alfama and Mouraria. The word for its mood is saudade, longing for something gone or never had. Amália Rodrigues took it to the world in the 1950s, and UNESCO listed it in 2011.
chapters.tip: Fado houses start late, often after 9 p.m. When a fadista sings, the room goes quiet and stays that way.

chapters.heading: Deep song across the river
chapters.text: Triana, across the Guadalquivir from the cathedral, was home to Gitano families, potters, and sailors. The oldest flamenco, cante jondo or “deep song,” is about grief, prison, and hunger. Niña de los Peines recorded it in the 1910s, when most of it had never been written down.
chapters.tip: Tablaos are shows for visitors. Peñas, members’ clubs that often let in guests, are where locals listen.

chapters.heading: Songs for the people who left
chapters.text: Millions of Neapolitans emigrated to the Americas, and many of the city’s songs were written for them. “Santa Lucia luntana” is sung from a ship pulling out of the bay. “Munasterio ’e Santa Chiara,” from 1945, asks whether it’s true that Naples has been destroyed, after Allied bombs burned the church.

chapters.heading: One song, played everywhere
chapters.text: Rezső Seress wrote “Szomorú vasárnap” in 1933 and played piano most nights at the Kispipa in the old Jewish quarter. Translated as “Gloomy Sunday,” it went around the world, and the press gave it a reputation as cursed. Billie Holiday’s 1941 version is the best known in English.
chapters.image: Akácfa utca a Rákóczi út felől nézve. Fortepan 15309.jpg

chapters.heading: Refugees in the port
chapters.text: After 1922 more than a million Greeks were expelled from Asia Minor, and many ended up in shanty towns around Piraeus. They brought the music of Smyrna’s cafés, and in the port’s hash dens it became rebetiko: bouzouki songs about exile, prison, drugs, and love. The Metaxas dictatorship censored it in the 1930s.

chapters.heading: The voice of the old taverns
chapters.text: Maria Tănase sang the songs of Romania’s lăutari, the mostly Roma musicians who played in taverns and at weddings. She was a star from the late 1930s to her death in 1963, and many Romanians still know her songs by heart.

chapters.heading: Songs for the new arrivals
chapters.text: From the 1960s, millions moved from the Anatolian countryside to Istanbul and built houses on its edges overnight. Arabesk, with Turkish folk tunes, Egyptian strings, and lyrics about fate and heartbreak, was their music. State radio kept it off the air for years. It sold on cassettes from the wholesale blocks at Unkapanı.

title: Jazz in Europe
intro: Jazz arrived in Europe with American soldiers and touring bands after the First World War, and Black American musicians soon found they were treated better in Paris than at home. Within a generation every city had its own players.
Under communism in Poland it was first banned and then tolerated, which made it sound like freedom.

chapters.heading: Le jazz hot
chapters.text: In the 1920s Black American musicians filled the clubs of Montmartre. Josephine Baker arrived in 1925 with the Revue Nègre and became the biggest star in Paris, dancing at the Folies Bergère.
chapters.image: Josephine Baker, Amerikaans,Franse artieste, in de Folies Bergère tijdens een optreden, SFA001007973.jpg

chapters.heading: Banjo
chapters.text: Claude McKay, a Harlem Renaissance writer, set his 1929 novel Banjo on the Marseille docks, among Black sailors and drifters from Africa, America, and the Caribbean who played music for whatever they could get.

chapters.heading: Jazz in Pera
chapters.text: In the years when Constantinople became Istanbul, Russian refugees and visiting bands brought jazz to the nightclubs and hotel ballrooms of Pera, the European quarter above the Golden Horn.

chapters.heading: Ježek
chapters.text: Jaroslav Ježek wrote jazzy songs and dance numbers for Prague’s satirical Liberated Theatre. He was almost blind and composed in an apartment painted deep blue to ease his eyes. He left for New York in 1939 and died there in 1942.

chapters.heading: Django
chapters.text: Django Reinhardt, a Romani guitarist who played with two fingers on his fretting hand after a fire, wrote Nuages in occupied Paris in 1940. His style, gypsy jazz, still plays in the bars of the Saint-Ouen flea market.

chapters.heading: Monica Zetterlund
chapters.text: Stockholm had one of Europe’s liveliest jazz scenes, centered on the Nalen hall. Monica Zetterlund sang American standards with Swedish words and in 1964 recorded an album with the pianist Bill Evans.

chapters.heading: Bluesette
chapters.text: Toots Thielemans, born above a café in the Marolles, played harmonica and guitar, and could whistle along with his own guitar lines. His 1962 waltz Bluesette became a jazz standard.

chapters.heading: Americans in Copenhagen
chapters.text: In the 1960s American players like Dexter Gordon and Ben Webster settled in Copenhagen, where they found steady work and less racism. At Jazzhus Montmartre the teenage bassist Niels-Henning Ørsted Pedersen backed them night after night.

chapters.heading: Polish jazz
chapters.text: In Stalinist Poland jazz was banned and played in private, the “catacomb” years. After 1956 it came into the open. Krzysztof Komeda recorded Astigmatic in Warsaw in 1965, and in Kraków Tomasz Stańko and the violinist Zbigniew Seifert took it further out.

chapters.heading: Garden Party
chapters.text: A group of Reykjavík schoolfriends called Mezzoforte made a jazz-funk instrumental that reached the British top 20 in 1983, the first time many people heard music from Iceland.

title: Punk
intro: Punk started in London in 1976 and spread across Europe within a couple of years: three chords, cheap clubs, home-made records. In most cities it was also about something local, from boredom to the Troubles.
The stops run roughly in the order punk arrived.

chapters.heading: Year zero
chapters.text: Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood’s shop at 430 King’s Road dressed the Sex Pistols. The scene played the 100 Club and the Roxy, and by 1977 the Clash were singing about London itself.

chapters.heading: Forty people
chapters.text: In June 1976 the Sex Pistols played the Lesser Free Trade Hall to a small crowd. Members of Buzzcocks, Joy Division, and the Fall were there, or said they were, and Manchester’s bands came out of it.

chapters.heading: Good Vibrations
chapters.text: In Belfast during the Troubles, punk was one of the few scenes Catholic and Protestant kids shared. Terri Hooley’s Good Vibrations record shop put out records by local bands, including the Undertones’ “Teenage Kicks.”

chapters.heading: Ça plane pour moi
chapters.text: Plastic Bertrand’s “Ça plane pour moi” was a Europe-wide hit in 1977, a novelty punk single fronted by a Belgian drummer.

chapters.heading: Zurich burns
chapters.text: Zurich’s punk band Kleenex, later LiLiPUT, were four women whose records came out on Rough Trade in London. In 1980 young people rioted for a cultural center of their own, and got the Rote Fabrik.

chapters.heading: West Berlin
chapters.text: In walled-in West Berlin, Kreuzberg’s SO36 club was the center of the punk and post-punk scene. Nina Hagen had come over from the East in 1976.

chapters.heading: Ebba Grön
chapters.text: Ebba Grön came out of a youth center in the Stockholm suburb of Rågsved. “Staten och kapitalet,” the state and capital, became a protest anthem.

chapters.heading: Rokk í Reykjavík
chapters.text: Iceland’s punk scene was tiny but loud. Purrkur Pillnikk and other bands appear in the 1982 film Rokk í Reykjavík. Jón Gnarr, a teenage punk at the time, became the city’s mayor in 2010.

title: Electronic music
intro: Synthesizers came out of studios in West Berlin, Paris, and Munich in the 1970s. By the end of the 1980s their sound had moved into clubs in Manchester and London, and after the Wall fell, Berlin’s empty buildings filled with techno.
Most of the places here are clubs and studios, some of them long gone.

chapters.heading: Tangerine Dream
chapters.text: In walled-in West Berlin, Tangerine Dream made long, slow pieces on synthesizers and sequencers. Albums like Stratosfear, from 1976, laid down a sound later heard in every Berlin club.

chapters.heading: Oxygène
chapters.text: Jean-Michel Jarre recorded Oxygène in a home studio, and it sold millions. He later played giant free concerts, including one on the Place de la Concorde in 1979.

chapters.heading: I Feel Love
chapters.text: In a studio under a Munich tower block, Giorgio Moroder and Pete Bellotte built I Feel Love for Donna Summer almost entirely on a Moog synthesizer. Its pulsing bassline seeded house and techno.

chapters.heading: Belgian electronics
chapters.text: Brussels had Telex, a deadpan synth-pop trio, and then Front 242, who called their harsh, marching sound electronic body music. Both fed straight into techno.

chapters.heading: The Haçienda
chapters.text: New Order put royalties from Blue Monday into a huge club, the Haçienda, in 1982. Hardly anyone danced at first. Then acid house arrived in 1988, along with local records like Voodoo Ray, and the Haçienda became the center of it. It lost money the whole time and closed in 1997.

chapters.heading: Soul II Soul
chapters.text: Soul II Soul started as a sound system playing Sunday nights at the Africa Centre in Covent Garden. Their slow, heavy Back to Life went to number one in 1989.

chapters.heading: After the Wall
chapters.text: West Berlin DJs had been playing house and techno through the 1980s. When the Wall came down, the empty buildings of East Berlin became clubs, and the Love Parade grew from 150 people in 1989 to over a million. Berghain, in a former power station, opened in 2004.

chapters.heading: French touch
chapters.text: In the 1990s Daft Punk and their peers made filtered, disco-flavored house that the press called French touch. The Rex Club, a basement on the Grands Boulevards, was its home.

chapters.heading: Levels
chapters.text: Tim Bergling, a young producer from Stockholm who called himself Avicii, became one of the biggest names in the global dance boom with Levels. He died in 2018, and the city’s arena was renamed after him.

chapters.heading: Glue
chapters.text: The Belfast duo Bicep grew up going to Shine, a club night at Queen’s University. Their 2017 track Glue is about missing the raves of the 1990s.

title: Eurovision
intro: The Eurovision Song Contest started in 1956 with seven countries. It has launched a few global careers, started at least one revolution, and become the place where Europe argues about itself in three-minute songs.
This thread follows a handful of entries back to the cities that sent them.

chapters.heading: Waterloo
chapters.text: ABBA won in Brighton in April 1974 with Waterloo and became one of the biggest-selling groups ever. Their whole story is in a museum on the island of Djurgården.

chapters.heading: A song as a signal
chapters.text: Portugal’s 1974 entry, E Depois do Adeus, came near the bottom. Three weeks later a radio station played it late on April 24 as the first signal for army officers to start a coup against the dictatorship. The second signal, after midnight, was the banned folk song Grândola, Vila Morena.

chapters.heading: Rise Like a Phoenix
chapters.text: Conchita Wurst, the bearded drag persona of Tom Neuwirth, won for Austria in 2014 with a Bond-style ballad and a speech about tolerance. Vienna hosted the contest the next year.

chapters.heading: Portugal finally wins
chapters.text: After more than fifty years of trying, Portugal won in 2017 with Salvador Sobral’s quiet ballad Amar Pelos Dois, written by his sister. Lisbon hosted the contest in 2018.

chapters.heading: Soldi
chapters.text: Mahmood grew up in Gratosoglio, a high-rise housing project on Milan’s southern edge. Soldi, about a father who left, includes a line in Arabic. It came second in 2019.

chapters.heading: Måneskin
chapters.text: Måneskin started as teenagers busking on Via del Corso. They won in 2021 with a glam-rock song, the first Italian win since 1990, and went on to tour the world.
chapters.image: Crowds on Via del Corso on a weekend afternoon November 2024.jpg

chapters.heading: In corpore sano
chapters.text: Serbia won in 2007, and Belgrade hosted the next year. In 2022 Konstrakta, an architect turned performer, sat at a basin washing her hands and sang deadpan about health care and beauty standards. It came fifth.

chapters.heading: Cha Cha Cha
chapters.text: Finland won in 2006 with the monster-masked rock band Lordi. In 2023 Käärijä, in a bolero of bright green sleeves, won the public vote with a song about drinking away the working week, and came second overall. His home town painted a mural of him.
chapters.image: Käärijä Eurovision Song Contest Final 2024 interval act.jpg

title: Writers’ cities
intro: Some books are inseparable from the city they were written in. You can stand where Bloom bought his soap or where Kafka filed his reports.
Each stop is one writer and the building or street most tied to them.

chapters.heading: Cervantes in jail
chapters.text: Miguel de Cervantes spent years in Seville as a tax collector and in 1597 was jailed in the Royal Prison on Calle Sierpes over missing money. In the prologue to Don Quixote he says the book was born in a prison. The thieves and card sharps of his Exemplary Stories work the same streets.

chapters.heading: Shakespeare’s Bankside
chapters.text: The Globe opened on the south bank of the Thames in 1599, among bear pits and brothels outside the City’s control. Shakespeare wrote Hamlet, King Lear, and Macbeth for it. It burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during Henry VIII set the thatch alight. The reconstruction opened nearby in 1997.

chapters.heading: Burns comes to town
chapters.text: Robert Burns arrived in Edinburgh in 1786, a plowman from Ayrshire whose first book of poems had just made him famous. The city’s salons took him up for a season. The Writers’ Museum, in a close off the Royal Mile, keeps his desk along with relics of Walter Scott and Robert Louis Stevenson.
chapters.image: Edinburgh - Edinburgh, Lawnmarket, Lady Stair's Close, Lady Stair's House - 20140421142708.jpg

chapters.heading: Andersen
chapters.text: Hans Christian Andersen, a cobbler’s son, came to Copenhagen at fourteen to be an actor and failed. He wrote The Little Mermaid, The Snow Queen, and more than 150 other tales instead, and lived in three different houses on Nyhavn.

chapters.heading: Ibsen comes home
chapters.text: Henrik Ibsen wrote A Doll’s House and Ghosts in Italy and Germany, in a self-imposed exile of 27 years. He came back to Kristiania, now Oslo, in 1891, walked every day to the Grand Café, and spent his last years in an apartment on Arbins gate, now a museum.

chapters.heading: One day in Dublin
chapters.text: James Joyce left Dublin in 1904 and never lived there again, but Ulysses follows one day there, June 16, 1904, street by street. It opens in the Martello tower at Sandycove. Leopold Bloom buys lemon soap at Sweny’s, which still sells it. Bloomsday is celebrated on the date every year.
chapters.image: Sweny's pharmacy, Lincoln Place, Dublin, Ireland 11.jpg

chapters.heading: Kafka at the office
chapters.text: Franz Kafka spent fourteen years as a lawyer at the Workers’ Accident Insurance Institute, assessing injury claims and writing reports on factory safety. He wrote at night: The Metamorphosis, The Trial, The Castle. Before he died in 1924 he asked his friend Max Brod to burn the manuscripts. Brod published them.
chapters.image: Na poříčí, Na Florenci, od Těšnova.jpg

chapters.heading: Pessoa’s many names
chapters.text: Fernando Pessoa worked as a commercial translator in Lisbon and wrote under dozens of invented names, each with its own biography and style. Almost none of it was published in his lifetime. After he died a trunk of more than 25,000 pages was found. His last apartment in Campo de Ourique is now a museum.

chapters.heading: Hemingway’s Paris
chapters.text: Ernest Hemingway lived in Paris in the early 1920s as a newspaper correspondent, borrowing books from Sylvia Beach’s Shakespeare and Company and writing in cafés. A Moveable Feast, published after his death, is his account of those years. The present shop by Notre-Dame took the name in 1964.

chapters.heading: Szymborska
chapters.text: Wisława Szymborska lived most of her life in Kraków, at first in the communal writers’ house on Krupnicza Street. She published few poems, short and dry and funny, and won the Nobel Prize in 1996. She found the fame that followed hard to bear.
chapters.image: Krupnicza street, view to W, Kraków, Poland.jpg

image: The interior of Sweny's pharmacy, Lincoln Place, Dublin, Ireland 02.jpg

title: Scientists
intro: Many of the ideas that changed how we see the world were worked out in a few European rooms, often by people who had to move to find them.
The stops follow science from Copernicus’s student years to Bohr’s institute in occupied Copenhagen.

chapters.heading: Copernicus
chapters.text: Nicolaus Copernicus studied at the university in Kraków in the early 1490s, where astronomy was taught well. Half a century later his book arguing that the earth goes around the sun was published as he died, in 1543. The university’s oldest building, the Collegium Maius, keeps instruments from his time.

chapters.heading: Tycho and Kepler
chapters.text: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, who had lost part of his nose in a duel, came to Prague in 1599 as Rudolf II’s imperial mathematician. He hired a young Johannes Kepler and died in 1601. Kepler used Tycho’s observations to work out that the planets move in ellipses. Tycho is buried in the Týn Church.

chapters.heading: Galileo’s telescopes
chapters.text: Galileo turned a telescope on the sky in 1609 and found four moons circling Jupiter. He named them after the Medici, and the next year they made him court mathematician in Florence. Two of his telescopes are in the Museo Galileo, along with a finger taken from his body when it was moved in 1737.
chapters.image: Galilei telescopes, Museo Galileo, Florence, Inv. 242, 2428, 224088.jpg

chapters.heading: Longitude
chapters.text: Charles II founded the Royal Observatory in 1675 to chart the stars well enough for ships to find their longitude. Christopher Wren, an astronomer before he was an architect, designed it. From 1833 a ball on its roof dropped every day at one o’clock so ships on the Thames could set their clocks. In 1884 the world agreed to measure longitude from here.
chapters.image: View of the Royal Observatory Greenwich from One Tree Hill in Greenwich Park, London, 20260719 0940 4508.jpg

chapters.place: Vinterviken and the Nobel Prize Museum, Stockholm
chapters.heading: Nobel
chapters.text: Alfred Nobel’s experiments with nitroglycerin killed his younger brother in Stockholm in 1864, and the city banned him. He moved his work to a barge and then to Vinterviken, invented dynamite, and grew rich. His will left most of his fortune to prizes, first awarded in 1901.

chapters.heading: Maria Skłodowska
chapters.text: Maria Skłodowska was born on Freta Street in 1867, in Russian-ruled Warsaw, and studied at the illegal Flying University because women could not go to the real one. She moved to Paris in 1891. As Marie Curie she won the Nobel Prize for physics in 1903 and for chemistry in 1911.

chapters.heading: Freud
chapters.text: Sigmund Freud lived and saw patients at Berggasse 19 for 47 years. The Interpretation of Dreams came out in 1899. In 1938, after Germany annexed Austria, he left for London with the famous couch. The Vienna apartment is a museum; the couch is in London.

chapters.heading: Einstein
chapters.text: Albert Einstein trained as a physics teacher at the Zurich Polytechnic, now ETH, from 1896, and could not get an academic job after. He wrote his papers of 1905, including special relativity, while working in the patent office in Bern. Zurich gave him professorships in 1909 and 1912 before he left for Berlin.

chapters.heading: The nucleus
chapters.text: Ernest Rutherford ran the physics laboratory at Manchester for twelve years. In 1911 he showed that an atom has a tiny, dense nucleus, from experiments firing particles at gold foil, and in 1917 he became the first to change one element into another. Graphene was isolated in the same university in 2004.
chapters.image: Front Entrance of the Rutherford building.jpg

chapters.heading: Bohr’s institute
chapters.text: Niels Bohr’s institute on Blegdamsvej opened in 1921 and became the center of quantum physics, with young physicists visiting from all over the world. In September 1941 Werner Heisenberg, by then working on Germany’s atomic program, came to see Bohr in occupied Copenhagen. Nobody knows exactly what was said. Bohr escaped to Sweden in 1943.

image: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump.jpg

title: The Enlightenment
intro: In the century after 1700, a loose network of writers and thinkers across Europe argued that reason, evidence, and open debate should decide things, rather than tradition, kings, or the church.

They called their age the Enlightenment. This thread follows the idea from a banned philosopher in Amsterdam to the salons of Paris, a Scottish city that briefly led the world in thinking, and one philosopher who left his body on display in London.
image: Anicet-Charles-Gabriel Lemonnier - In the Salon of Madame Geoffrin in 1755 - WGA12652.jpg

chapters.heading: A philosopher thrown out at 23
chapters.text: The story starts before the century did, in Amsterdam. In the 1600s the Dutch Republic, as the Netherlands was then called, was one of the few places in Europe where unusual ideas could be printed. Baruch Spinoza grew up there in a family of Portuguese Jews who had fled persecution in Iberia. In 1656, when he was 23, his community expelled him for his views, and it never took him back. He earned a modest living grinding lenses and kept writing. He argued that God and nature are the same thing, and that a state should let people think and speak freely. Most of his work was published only after his death in 1677, and it was banned across Europe. It was read anyway.

mediaNote.lead: Spinoza is hard to read, so here are two easier ways in.
items: A radio discussion among academics explains what he argued and why it frightened people.
A short, personal book by a modern philosopher tells the story of his expulsion.

chapters.heading: A book of all knowledge
chapters.text: By the middle of the 1700s the center of the argument had moved to Paris. There, the writer Denis Diderot and the mathematician Jean d’Alembert set out to gather everything known about the world into one work, the Encyclopédie. It covered science and philosophy, but also trades like weaving and printing, as if a craftsman’s knowledge mattered as much as a priest’s. The French crown banned it in 1759, and the volumes kept coming out anyway. Its ideas were argued over in salons, the regular gatherings that wealthy women held in their drawing rooms. Voltaire, the most famous writer of the age, spent years in exile for mocking the church and the state. In 1791, during the Revolution, his remains were moved to the Panthéon, a church turned into a burial place for the nation’s great figures.

mediaNote.lead: Two pieces take you to Enlightenment Paris.
items: A walking tour of the Latin Quarter passes the Panthéon, where Voltaire is buried.
A short video looks at The Oath of the Horatii, a painting by Jacques-Louis David that caught the mood of Paris a few years before the Revolution.

chapters.heading: A king who wanted to be a philosopher
chapters.text: Some rulers liked the new ideas, or liked being seen to. Frederick the Great, king of Prussia, the powerful German state centered on Berlin, wrote poetry, played the flute, and corresponded with Voltaire. Soon after taking the throne in 1740 he largely abolished torture, and he allowed religions that other states persecuted. In Potsdam, just outside Berlin, he built a small summer palace and named it Sanssouci, French for “without worries.” Voltaire came to live at his court in 1750. Within three years the two men had quarreled, and Voltaire left. Frederick also spent much of his reign at war, and he showed that a ruler could talk like a philosopher and still act like a king.

items: For the whole contradictory man, there is a radio discussion about his wars, his writing, and his court at Sanssouci.

chapters.heading: An earthquake tests the age
chapters.text: On the morning of November 1, 1755, a great earthquake struck Lisbon, followed by a tsunami and fires that burned for days. Tens of thousands of people died. Across Europe, writers asked how a loving God could allow it. Voltaire wrote a long poem about the disaster, and later Candide, a comic novel that mocks the idea that we live in the best of all possible worlds. In Lisbon itself, the king’s chief minister, the man later known as the Marquis of Pombal, answered with planning. He had the old center rebuilt on a straight grid of streets, with buildings framed in wood so they would sway rather than fall in the next quake.

items: To see what Pombal built, there is a short video about how he rebuilt the city after the earthquake.

chapters.place: Dr. Johnson’s House, Gough Square, London
chapters.heading: Knowledge for the public
chapters.text: In London the new spirit was less about philosophy and more about information. In a narrow house off Fleet Street, the writer Samuel Johnson spent nine years compiling the first great dictionary of English, published in 1755. Science was becoming public too. Traveling lecturers carried instruments from town to town and performed experiments for paying audiences. In 1768 the painter Joseph Wright of Derby showed one of them at work, pumping the air out of a glass bowl while a family watches a bird inside it struggle to breathe.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into that London.
items: A lively book describes the London Johnson lived in, from the gin to the wigs.
A short episode takes a slow look at Wright’s painting, which hangs in the National Gallery.

chapters.image: Dr Johnsons House - 17 Gough Square, City of London (4043340189).jpg

chapters.heading: Edinburgh’s great half-century
chapters.text: For a few decades, the boldest thinking in Europe came from Edinburgh, then a crowded, poor city. The philosopher David Hume argued that we can never prove that one thing causes another, and that much of what we believe rests on habit. His friend Adam Smith studied how trade and markets work, and in 1776 he published The Wealth of Nations, one of the founding books of economics. Smith spent his last years in a house on the Canongate, at the bottom of the Royal Mile, where he gathered friends for supper on Sundays. A statue of Hume now stands on the Royal Mile, and visitors rub its toe for luck, which Hume would have found funny.

mediaNote.lead: Four pieces go further into Edinburgh’s thinkers.
items: A short episode starts at Hume’s statue and explains his ideas.
An economics podcast asks what Adam Smith can still teach us.
A history book tells how this small city came to lead the world in thinking.
A walking tour follows the thinkers through the Old Town.

chapters.image: 6. Bronze statue of philosopher David Hume (1711-1776 CE), by Alexander Stoddart. Royal Mile, Edinburgh, Scotland, UK.jpg

chapters.heading: Reform from the top, for sixteen months
chapters.text: The new ideas could also be imposed from above. In 1770 Johann Struensee, a German doctor treating the mentally ill king of Denmark, became the real power at court. In sixteen months he issued hundreds of decrees in the king’s name. He ended censorship of the press, one of the first rulers in Europe to do so, and abolished torture. He also had an affair with the queen. In January 1772 a group of nobles arrested him after a masked ball, and three months later he was executed.

mediaNote.lead: Struensee’s story is told two ways.
items: A history podcast tells the story from the masked ball to the scaffold.
A Danish film dramatizes the affair and the reforms.

chapters.heading: A philosopher on display
chapters.text: The age ended with a joke that was also an argument. Jeremy Bentham, a London philosopher, believed that laws should aim at the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people, and that old customs had no special authority. He thought dead bodies should be useful, not just buried. When he died in 1832, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes and seated in a wooden cabinet, as he had asked. It still sits at University College London, with a wax head. The real one is kept in storage.

items: For the whole strange story, there is a short video about how his body ended up on display.

title: Fire, flood, and earthquake
intro: Cities burn, flood, and shake, and some of the ones we visit were shaped by the disaster as much as by any architect. London’s skyline after 1666 and Lisbon’s grid after 1755 were both built on ruins.
The most recent of these is still being dealt with, by steel gates under the sea.

chapters.heading: Rome burns
chapters.text: A fire broke out near the Circus Maximus in July 64 and burned for six days. The story of Nero fiddling while it burned is a later invention, but he did use the cleared land for a vast new palace.

chapters.heading: Vesuvius
chapters.text: In 79 Vesuvius buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash and hot gas. The towns lay hidden until the 1700s. Loaves found still in a baker’s oven are in the archaeological museum in Naples.

chapters.place: Pudding Lane and the Monument, London
chapters.heading: The Great Fire
chapters.text: In September 1666 a fire started in a bakery on Pudding Lane and burned for four days, destroying most of the medieval City, including St. Paul’s Cathedral. Christopher Wren rebuilt St. Paul’s and designed the Monument near where the fire began.

chapters.heading: All Saints’ Day
chapters.text: On the morning of November 1, 1755, an earthquake flattened much of Lisbon, then a tsunami came up the river and fires burned for days. Tens of thousands died. The Marquis of Pombal rebuilt the lower town on a grid, with buildings framed to survive the next one. The Carmo Convent was left as a ruin.

chapters.heading: The Seine floods
chapters.text: In January 1910 the Seine rose about eight meters and flooded streets, cellars, and Métro tunnels for weeks. Parisians still judge floods by how far up the stone Zouave soldier on the Pont de l’Alma the water reaches.
chapters.image: Crue de la Seine. Rue Surcouf, 7ème arrondissement, Paris, le 28 janvier 1910. PH3201.jpg

chapters.heading: Vesuvius again
chapters.text: In March 1944, with Allied troops already in Naples, Vesuvius erupted for eleven days. Lava swallowed the village of San Sebastiano, and falling ash wrecked dozens of American bombers at a nearby airfield.

chapters.heading: The Arno floods
chapters.text: On November 4, 1966, the Arno burst its banks and filled Florence with mud and fuel oil. Volunteers from around the world, the “mud angels,” came to dig out books and paintings. Cimabue’s crucifix in Santa Croce was among the worst damaged.
chapters.image: National Library manuscripts being washed in Florence after the 1966 flood of the Arno - UNESCO - PHOTO 0000001407 0001 - Restoration.jpg

chapters.heading: The 1977 earthquake
chapters.text: On March 4, 1977, an earthquake killed about 1,500 people, most of them in Bucharest, where interwar apartment blocks along the main boulevards collapsed. Ceaușescu used the damage as a reason for the demolitions that followed.

chapters.heading: High water
chapters.text: The same day the Arno flooded Florence, the highest tide on record flooded Venice. After decades of delay, a line of steel gates on the seabed, called MOSE, began rising to close the lagoon in 2020. St. Mark’s Square, the lowest part of the city, still floods most often.
chapters.image: San Marco, Acqua Alta - Venice, Italy - panoramio.jpg

title: Exiles
intro: Europe’s cities have always taken in people who couldn’t go home: poets thrown out by rivals, revolutionaries waiting for their moment, refugees from war. Some places became waiting rooms where people sat for months for a visa or a ship.
This thread follows exiles from Dante to people arriving now.

chapters.heading: Dante
chapters.text: In 1302 Dante was exiled from Florence by a rival faction and sentenced to be burned if he came back. He never returned and wrote the Divine Comedy in exile, putting several of his enemies in hell. He died in Ravenna in 1321.

chapters.heading: Lenin, Joyce, and Dada
chapters.text: Neutral Switzerland filled with refugees and draft dodgers in the First World War. On one short street in Zurich’s old town, artists founded Dada at the Cabaret Voltaire while Lenin lived a few doors up. James Joyce was writing Ulysses across town. In April 1917 Lenin left by train for Russia.

chapters.heading: A passport for the stateless
chapters.text: The polar explorer Fridtjof Nansen became the League of Nations’ high commissioner for refugees. In 1922 he created the Nansen passport, a travel document for people who had lost their citizenship, and won the Nobel Peace Prize.

chapters.heading: The exchange
chapters.text: After Greece’s defeat in Anatolia, Greece and Turkey agreed in 1923 to swap their minorities by religion. More than a million Orthodox Christians came to Greece. In Athens they built new districts and named them after the towns they had lost, like Nea Smyrni and Nea Ionia.

chapters.heading: Leaving Vienna
chapters.text: After Germany annexed Austria in March 1938, tens of thousands of Viennese Jews fled, leaving homes and art to be taken. Maria Altmann was one of them. Decades later she won back Klimt’s portrait of her aunt, which had hung in the Belvedere.
chapters.image: Palacio Belvedere, Viena, Austria, 2020-02-01, DD 93-95 HDR.jpg

chapters.heading: Marseille
chapters.text: When France fell, refugees crowded into Marseille looking for visas and ships. The American journalist Varian Fry helped about 2,000 people get out, among them Chagall, Hannah Arendt, and André Breton. Anna Seghers turned the waiting into the novel Transit.

chapters.heading: The last port
chapters.text: Neutral Portugal was the way out of Europe for many who made it across Spain. Refugees waited in Lisbon’s cafés for a place on a ship to America, sometimes for months.
chapters.image: Westward view from the south end of Rossio, Lisbon, 2010.jpg

chapters.heading: Brodsky’s winters
chapters.text: The Soviet Union expelled the poet Joseph Brodsky in 1972. He settled in the US but spent most winters in Venice and wrote a short book about it. He is buried on the cemetery island of San Michele.

chapters.heading: Arriving now
chapters.text: The war in Syria sent more than a million people to Europe in 2015 and 2016. One Syrian filmmaker recorded his arrival at Amsterdam Centraal. In Paris, a workshop gives exiled artists space and tools.

title: Plague cities
intro: The Black Death killed about a third of Europe’s people in the 1340s, and plague kept coming back for nearly four hundred years. Cities invented quarantine, built churches to give thanks for surviving, and left monuments that are still there.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: The Decameron
chapters.text: Plague reached Florence in 1348 and killed perhaps half the city. Boccaccio’s Decameron opens with seven young women meeting three young men at Santa Maria Novella and leaving town to tell each other stories while it passes.

chapters.heading: Quarantine
chapters.text: Venice set up the first permanent plague hospital on an island in 1423 and kept ships and goods waiting forty days, quaranta giorni. After the plague of 1630–31 it built Santa Maria della Salute to give thanks.
chapters.image: (Venice) - Santa Maria della Salute - Le due cupole e i due campanili.jpg

chapters.heading: The Betrothed
chapters.text: The plague of 1630 killed about half of Milan. Alessandro Manzoni set the climax of The Betrothed, Italy’s best-known novel, in the city’s lazzaretto, with crowds blaming “anointers” for spreading it.
chapters.image: Dal Re, Marc'Antonio (1697-1766) - Vedute di Milano - Il lazzaretto.jpg

chapters.heading: The Great Plague
chapters.text: London’s last great plague killed about a fifth of the city in 1665. Samuel Pepys recorded it in his diary, and then the Great Fire of 1666.
chapters.image: Monument to the Great Fire of London EC3R 8AH.jpg

chapters.heading: The skulls of Fontanelle
chapters.text: The plague of 1656 killed about half of Naples. Many of the dead ended up in a quarry in the Sanità district, later a cemetery. Neapolitans adopted the skulls there and cared for them in return for favors.

chapters.heading: The last great outbreak
chapters.text: In 1720 a ship carrying plague was let into Marseille’s port, reportedly because the merchants who owned its cargo pushed to skip quarantine. Around half the city died. It was the last major plague outbreak in Western Europe.

image: The Triumph of Death by Pieter Bruegel the Elder.jpg

title: Jewish quarters
intro: Jews have lived in European cities for more than two thousand years. In many of them, the Jewish quarter was where they were allowed or required to live, and its streets, synagogues, and cemeteries are among the oldest parts of town.
This thread goes roughly in the order the communities were founded. It includes the Holocaust, but it starts long before it, and in some cities it does not end with it.

chapters.heading: The oldest community
chapters.text: Rome’s Jewish community is the oldest in Europe. The Arch of Titus shows Roman soldiers carrying the menorah looted from Jerusalem in 70 AD. In 1555 a pope walled Rome’s Jews into a ghetto by the Tiber, which lasted until 1870. On October 16, 1943, the Germans rounded up more than a thousand people there; sixteen came back.
chapters.tip: Restaurants along Via del Portico d’Ottavia serve carciofi alla giudia, whole artichokes fried twice.

chapters.heading: Sepharad
chapters.text: Santa Cruz, now the most photographed quarter of Seville, was its judería. In 1391 riots against the Jews started here and spread across Spain. In 1492 the Jews who had not converted were expelled from the country.

chapters.heading: The first ghetto
chapters.text: In 1516 Venice ordered its Jews to live on a small island by an old foundry, a getto, which was locked at night. The word spread to the rest of Europe. With no room to expand, the buildings grew up to seven stories, taller than anywhere else in the city.

chapters.heading: A refuge
chapters.text: Jews who had been forced to convert in Spain and Portugal found in Amsterdam a city where they could practice openly. Their Portuguese Synagogue opened in 1675 and is still lit by candles. In 1656 the community expelled one of its own, the philosopher Baruch Spinoza.

chapters.heading: The Old-New Synagogue
chapters.text: The Old-New Synagogue, from around 1270, is the oldest working synagogue in Europe. Legend says the clay Golem of Rabbi Loew lies in its attic. Next door, the Old Jewish Cemetery has graves up to twelve layers deep. Franz Kafka was born at the edge of the quarter.
chapters.image: Old New Synagogue- Jewish Town Hall (Prague).jpg

chapters.heading: Kazimierz
chapters.text: King Casimir founded Kazimierz as a separate town in 1335, and from 1495 Kraków’s Jews lived there. In 1941 the Germans moved them across the river into a ghetto in Podgórze. Since the 1990s Kazimierz has come back to life, with restored synagogues and an annual Jewish Culture Festival.
chapters.image: Wolf Popper Synagogue, Entrance gate, 16 Szeroka street, Kazimierz, Kraków, Poland.jpg

chapters.heading: The largest community in Europe
chapters.text: Before the war, about a third of Warsaw was Jewish. Isaac Bashevis Singer grew up on Krochmalna Street, and Janusz Korczak ran his orphanage nearby. In 1940 the Germans sealed off the ghetto. In April 1943 its last inhabitants rose up, and the Germans burned it street by street.

chapters.heading: Europe’s largest synagogue
chapters.text: The Dohány Street Synagogue, finished in 1859, seats about three thousand. Theodor Herzl, who imagined a Jewish state, was born next door. In 1944 Hungary’s Jews were deported in a few weeks; in Budapest, Raoul Wallenberg and other diplomats saved thousands with protective passes.

chapters.heading: A family’s netsuke
chapters.text: Vienna around 1900 was shaped by Jewish families: bankers, doctors, writers, composers. Edmund de Waal traced one of them, the Ephrussis, through a collection of Japanese netsuke hidden by a maid during the war. The Holocaust memorial on Judenplatz is a library whose books cannot be opened.

chapters.heading: Across the Sound
