chapters.text: When word came in 1943 that Denmark’s Jews were to be deported, ordinary Danes hid them and ferried about 7,000 across the water to neutral Sweden in a few weeks. Most of the community survived.

image: Old Jewish Cemetery in Josefov, Prague - 8363.jpg

title: The Atlantic slave trade
intro: For four centuries, European ships carried about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic to forced labor in the Americas. The trade was run from Europe’s ports, and the money built warehouses, banks, town halls, and country houses that are still there.
Each city here has started, at different speeds, to say so in public.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: Portuguese ships began taking captives from West Africa in the 1440s, and Portugal went on to carry more Africans across the Atlantic than any other country, mostly to Brazil. In the 1500s about one in ten people in Lisbon was Black.
chapters.image: Blue facades of waterfront buildings at Ribeira das Naus in Lisbon, Portugal, 20250604 2033 9639.jpg

chapters.heading: The Dutch West India Company
chapters.text: The Dutch West India Company, founded in 1621, traded in slaves from forts on the Gold Coast to colonies such as Suriname. The Netherlands abolished slavery in 1863, among the last in Western Europe. In 1934 the Surinamese writer Anton de Kom published a history of the colony told from the side of the enslaved.

chapters.heading: Denmark’s islands
chapters.text: Denmark held colonies in the Caribbean, now the US Virgin Islands, and shipped sugar and rum home to warehouses like this one on the harbor. It was the first country to pass a law banning the trade, in 1792, though it took effect only in 1803.

chapters.heading: The capital of the trade
chapters.text: London’s Royal African Company held a monopoly on the English slave trade from the 1670s, and the City financed and insured it. Black Londoners, free and enslaved, lived in the city throughout. The British Museum holds an Akan drum carried to Virginia in the 1700s.

chapters.heading: The biggest slaving port
chapters.text: By the end of the 1700s, Liverpool ships carried most of Britain’s trade in enslaved people. The money is in the street names, the Town Hall, and the old Exchange. Since 2007, the International Slavery Museum has stood on the dock where slaving ships were fitted out.

chapters.heading: Tobacco and sugar
chapters.text: Glasgow’s “tobacco lords” grew rich on plantations in Virginia and the Caribbean worked by enslaved people. Their mansions and warehouses are the Merchant City, and streets there are still called Virginia Street and Jamaica Street.

title: Spies
intro: For most of the 20th century, Europe’s cities were where spies met, traded secrets, and sometimes died. Neutral capitals, divided cities, and grand hotels were where the work got done.
This thread runs in date order, from a nurse shot in Brussels in the First World War to a poisoned cup of tea in London in 2006.

chapters.heading: A nurse before a firing squad
chapters.text: The story starts in the First World War, in Brussels, which the German army occupied in 1914. Edith Cavell, a British nurse, ran a nursing school and clinic in the city. With Belgian friends, she hid British and French soldiers who had been cut off behind the lines, and helped about two hundred of them escape to the neutral Netherlands. The Germans arrested her in 1915, and on October 12 she was shot by a firing squad at the Tir National, a shooting range on the edge of the city. Britain made her a martyr, and her face appeared on recruiting posters. For a long time she was remembered only as a nurse who saved lives. Some historians now argue that her network was also passing military intelligence to the British.

items: If you want the case for Cavell as a spy, there is a podcast episode in which a historian sets out the evidence.

chapters.heading: Orwell’s war
chapters.text: In the 1930s, Europe divided between fascism and communism, and the spying turned on ordinary people. In the Spanish Civil War, which began in 1936, the Soviet Union backed the Republic against General Franco, and it sent its secret police along too. George Orwell, the English writer, came to Barcelona to fight for the Republic. He joined the militia of the POUM, a small left-wing party that Moscow saw as an enemy. His wife, Eileen O’Shaughnessy, worked in Barcelona while he was at the front, in an office that looked after the British volunteers. In 1937 the POUM was banned and its members were arrested. Soviet-backed agents had been watching the couple, and they escaped to France in June, just in time.
chapters.image: 13 Edifici Telefònica, av. Portal de l'Àngel - pl. Catalunya (Barcelona).jpg

items: To hear her side of it, there is a podcast episode about Eileen running the office while Orwell fought, with informers all around her.

chapters.heading: The neutral port
chapters.text: When the Second World War began, Portugal stayed neutral, and Lisbon became one of the last open doors out of Europe. Refugees from across the continent crowded into the city, waiting for visas and a place on a ship to America. Spies came too. British and German agents watched each other in the same hotels and cafés, and in the casino at Estoril, a resort along the coast. Ian Fleming, then a British naval intelligence officer, passed through in 1941. The casino is said to have given him an idea for his first James Bond novel.

items: For a walk through it, there is a tour of the Baixa and Bairro Alto about the city’s rebuilding after the earthquake of 1755 and its wartime spies.

chapters.heading: The Third Man
chapters.text: After the war, the Cold War cut straight through some cities. Vienna, like Berlin, was divided between the four victorious powers: the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, and France. Soldiers from all four patrolled the old center together. The city was bombed out and short of everything, and a black market thrived. In 1948 the novelist Graham Greene and the director Carol Reed made The Third Man there. It is a thriller about an American writer searching for a friend who sells watered-down penicillin on the black market. Much of it was filmed in the real ruins, with a famous chase through the sewers and a meeting on the Riesenrad, the giant Ferris wheel in the Prater park.

items: If you have a free evening, the film itself is the best guide to postwar Vienna, and the Ferris wheel is still there to ride.

chapters.heading: The front line
chapters.text: Berlin was the front line. The city sat deep inside East Germany, divided between East and West, and from 1961 the Wall ran through it. Both sides filled it with agents. The Americans and British built a listening station on Teufelsberg, a hill in the west of the city made from the rubble of bombed buildings. From there they picked up radio traffic from the East. On the Glienicke Bridge, which crosses the river Havel between West Berlin and Potsdam, the two sides exchanged captured spies. The first swap came in 1962, when the Soviet agent Rudolf Abel was traded for Francis Gary Powers, an American pilot shot down over the Soviet Union. After East Germany collapsed in 1989, its citizens won the right to read the files the Stasi, the secret police, had kept on them.

mediaNote.lead: Berlin has more spy stories than any other stop, and here are four of them.
items: Steven Spielberg’s film Bridge of Spies tells the true story of the 1962 exchange, through the American lawyer who negotiated it.
A short radio report visits the abandoned listening station on Teufelsberg.
In a podcast episode, the director of the Allied Museum tells stories of espionage in the divided city.
And a historian at the Stasi Archives explains how the secret police worked, and how its files were saved.

chapters.heading: Radio across the Curtain
chapters.text: Not all Cold War spying was about stealing secrets. Some of it was about news. From 1951, Radio Free Europe, paid for by the American government, broadcast to Eastern Europe from a building on the edge of the English Garden, Munich’s large central park. Its sister station, Radio Liberty, broadcast to the Soviet Union from the same city. Communist governments jammed the signals and planted agents among the staff. In 1981 a bomb wrecked part of the Radio Free Europe building. It was later traced to a terrorist working for Romania’s secret police.

items: For a story from inside, there is a podcast episode in which a woman describes the day her husband, an editor at Radio Liberty, confessed that he had been spying for the KGB.

chapters.heading: Between the blocs
chapters.text: Between the two blocs sat Yugoslavia. Its leader, Josip Broz Tito, broke with Stalin in 1948 and refused to join either side, so both East and West courted him, and spied on him. That made Belgrade, the capital, a meeting ground. The café of the Hotel Moskva, a grand building from 1908 on Terazije, the city’s main square, was a favorite place for diplomats, journalists, and agents to watch one another. After Tito died in 1980, the country began to weaken, and the spying grew more urgent.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

items: To hear how it worked, there is a podcast episode in which a former CIA officer describes meeting a Yugoslav source in Belgrade’s cafés and hotels.

chapters.heading: Reading your own file
chapters.text: Some secret police spied mostly on their own people. In Romania under Nicolae Ceaușescu, the Securitate built one of the largest networks of informers in the Eastern bloc, and ordinary people learned to watch what they said. Foreigners were watched too. Katherine Verdery, an American anthropologist, did research in Romania from the 1970s. Years after the regime fell in 1989, she read the file the Securitate had kept on her. In it she appears as a spy, and she found that some of her friends had been informing on her.

items: If you want to read it, her book describes the file, the informers, and what happened when she went back to meet them.

chapters.heading: Polonium in Mayfair
chapters.text: The Cold War ended, but the spying did not. Alexander Litvinenko was a former officer of the FSB, Russia’s security service, who had accused his superiors of corruption and fled to London in 2000. On November 1, 2006, he had lunch at a sushi bar on Piccadilly, then met two Russian men for tea at the Millennium Hotel in Mayfair. Within hours he was ill. Doctors found he had been poisoned with polonium-210, a rare radioactive element, and he died three weeks later. In 2016 a British public inquiry concluded that the killing had probably been approved by President Vladimir Putin.

items: To hear the story from people close to it, there is a short Witness History episode about the poisoning.

title: Queer Europe
intro: For most of the twentieth century, gay men in Europe could be jailed for their relationships, and queer life went on in bars, magazines, and private clubs. In 1989 Denmark became the first country to recognize same-sex couples, and in 2015 Ireland voted for same-sex marriage.
This thread follows that change through the places where it happened.

chapters.heading: Weimar Berlin
chapters.text: In the 1920s the streets around Nollendorfplatz were full of gay and lesbian bars, and Magnus Hirschfeld ran an institute that studied sexuality. Christopher Isherwood lodged nearby and wrote the stories that became Cabaret. In May 1933 the Nazis ransacked the institute and burned its books.

chapters.heading: Sent away
chapters.text: Fascist Italy didn’t make homosexuality a crime but sent gay men into internal exile on remote islands. Ettore Scola’s film A Special Day takes place on the day Hitler visited Rome in 1938, when a housewife meets a neighbor about to be deported.

chapters.heading: Der Kreis
chapters.text: Switzerland legalized gay sex between adults in 1942. In Zurich, a club and magazine called Der Kreis held discreet dances and published in three languages, until a police crackdown in the 1960s broke it up.

chapters.heading: Alan Turing
chapters.text: The codebreaker, who worked on one of the first computers at Manchester University, was convicted of gross indecency in 1952 and given hormone treatment. He died two years later. A statue of him sits on a bench in Sackville Gardens, by the gay village.

chapters.heading: Tom of Finland
chapters.text: Touko Laaksonen, a war veteran working in advertising, drew muscular, cheerful gay men in a country where homosexuality was illegal until 1971. As Tom of Finland he became famous abroad long before he was accepted at home.
chapters.image: Statue of Johan Ludvig Runeberg on Esplanadi in Helsinki, Finland.jpg

chapters.heading: Pride
chapters.text: During the 1984 miners’ strike, a group of gay and lesbian activists raised money for a mining village in Wales. They met at Gay’s the Word bookshop. The miners later marched at London Pride.
chapters.image: Gay's the Word, London, Bloomsbury, WC1 b.jpg

chapters.heading: After Franco
chapters.text: Spain decriminalized homosexuality in 1979, a few years after Franco’s death. In the Movida, Madrid’s 1980s pop explosion, Alaska’s A quién le importa became an anthem, and Chueca grew into the city’s gay district.

chapters.heading: The first partnerships
chapters.text: On October 1, 1989, Denmark became the first country to let same-sex couples register their partnership. Eleven couples signed at Copenhagen City Hall that day, including the activists Axel and Eigil Axgil.

chapters.heading: The vote
chapters.text: Gay sex was illegal in Ireland until 1993. Twenty-two years later Ireland became the first country to allow same-sex marriage by popular vote, and crowds watched the result come in at Dublin Castle.
chapters.image: Dublin Castle Upper Castle Yard Panorama 01.jpg

title: Cities under bombs
intro: In the Second World War, bombing cities became a strategy rather than an accident. Warsaw, London, Belfast, Naples, and Berlin all spent months or years under air raids, and the ruins shaped how they were rebuilt.
This thread visits cities that were bombed and how they remember it.

chapters.heading: Warsaw
chapters.text: When Germany invaded Poland, its planes and artillery bombarded Warsaw for nearly three weeks. The Royal Castle burned, and the city surrendered on September 28. The castle was rebuilt in the 1970s.

chapters.heading: The Blitz
chapters.text: From September 1940 to May 1941 German bombers attacked London most nights. People sheltered in Tube stations, and Churchill’s government worked from a basement under Whitehall. In March 1943, 173 people were crushed on the stairs of the Bethnal Green station during an alert.

chapters.heading: The May Blitz
chapters.text: Liverpool’s docks were the main port for supplies from America, and it was the most bombed British city outside London. In the first week of May 1941, St. Luke’s Church burned out. It was left roofless as a memorial.
chapters.image: St. Luke's Church "Bombed out Church", Liverpool - geograph.org.uk - 7378089.jpg

chapters.heading: Belfast
chapters.text: Belfast had almost no shelters when German bombers came in April 1941. About 900 people died on Easter Tuesday, the most killed in one night anywhere in the UK outside London.

chapters.heading: Naples
chapters.text: Allied planes bombed Naples, Italy’s main southern port, again and again. Families sheltered in the ancient quarries and water tunnels under the city. Sophia Loren grew up in nearby Pozzuoli during the raids.

chapters.heading: A mistake
chapters.text: In March 1945 the RAF bombed the Gestapo’s headquarters in Copenhagen at the Danish resistance’s request. One plane crashed near a French school, and later planes bombed the fire by mistake. Eighty-six children were killed.

chapters.heading: Rubble
chapters.text: By 1945 bombing and the final battle had left much of Berlin in ruins. The broken tower of the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church was kept as a reminder, next to a new church built in the 1960s. Rossellini filmed the rubble in 1947.

chapters.heading: Belgrade
chapters.text: NATO bombed Yugoslavia for 78 days in 1999 over Kosovo. The army headquarters on Kneza Miloša street was hit and left as a ruin, and US bombs hit the Chinese embassy, killing three people.

title: Uprisings
intro: For forty-five years, people in Central and Eastern Europe kept trying to take their cities back. Most attempts were crushed within days or weeks. Each one was remembered, and in 1989 the anniversaries, the funerals, and the songs came back.
Each stop is a place you can still stand in.

chapters.heading: Warsaw rises
chapters.text: On August 1, 1944, the Polish Home Army attacked the German occupiers, hoping to free the city before the Red Army arrived. The Soviets stopped on the far bank of the Vistula and waited. The fighting lasted 63 days. Up to 200,000 civilians died, and the Germans then destroyed most of what was left of the city.
chapters.image: Warsaw Uprising - Soldiers from Parasol on Warecka Street.jpg

chapters.heading: Builders strike in East Berlin
chapters.text: Construction workers on Stalinallee walked off the job over higher work quotas. Within a day hundreds of thousands were protesting across East Germany. Soviet tanks put it down, and dozens were killed.
chapters.image: Bundesarchiv B 145 Bild-F005191-0040, Berlin, Aufstand, sowjetischer Panzer.jpg

chapters.heading: Budapest fights the tanks
chapters.text: A student march on October 23 ended with Stalin’s statue pulled down. Young fighters held the Corvin Passage against Soviet armor, and Prime Minister Imre Nagy announced that Hungary would leave the Warsaw Pact. On November 4 the Soviet army came back in force. About 2,500 Hungarians were killed and 200,000 fled the country. Nagy was hanged in 1958.
chapters.image: 1956, Budapest, Üllői út - Ferenc körút, Kilián laktanya.jpg

chapters.heading: Students against the censors
chapters.text: When the authorities closed a production of Mickiewicz’s play Dziady for being anti-Russian, students protested. The crackdown came with an antisemitic campaign that pushed about 13,000 Polish Jews to emigrate.

chapters.heading: The end of the Prague Spring
chapters.text: Alexander Dubček had promised “socialism with a human face”: less censorship, more debate. On the night of August 20, Warsaw Pact armies invaded. In January 1969 the student Jan Palach set himself on fire at the top of Wenceslas Square in protest. Marta Kubišová’s song “Modlitba pro Martu” became an anthem, and she was banned from performing for twenty years.
chapters.image: 10 Soviet Invasion of Czechoslovakia - Flickr - The Central Intelligence Agency.jpg

chapters.heading: A funeral, thirty-one years late
chapters.text: Hungary’s government agreed to rebury Imre Nagy with honors. About a quarter of a million people filled Heroes’ Square. It was the first sign that 1956 could be spoken about in public.

chapters.heading: The Wall opens
chapters.text: Erich Honecker had already been pushed out. At an evening press conference, a Politburo spokesman said the new travel rules applied “immediately.” Crowds went to the checkpoints, and at Bornholmer Straße the guards gave up and opened the gate.

chapters.heading: The Velvet Revolution
chapters.text: Police beat students on Národní street on November 17. Within days, Wenceslas Square filled every evening. Václav Havel spoke from the Melantrich balcony, and Marta Kubišová, banned since 1970, stood up there beside him. By the end of December Havel was president.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu’s last speech
chapters.text: On December 21 Nicolae Ceaușescu addressed a rally from the Central Committee balcony, and the crowd booed him on live television. He fled by helicopter the next day. He and his wife were tried and shot on December 25. Romania’s was the only revolution of 1989 with heavy bloodshed: more than a thousand people died.
chapters.image: PSL during the Romanian Revolution of 1989.jpg

image: Berlin 1989, Fall der Mauer, Chute du mur 10.jpg

intro: In 1968 protest moved across Europe in months, not years. Students in Warsaw and Paris, workers in France, reformers in Prague, and singers in Barcelona had different enemies, but they were watching each other.
The chapters follow the calendar.

chapters.heading: A banned play
chapters.text: The authorities closed a production of Mickiewicz’s Dziady for being anti-Russian. Students protested, police beat them at the university gate, and the government answered with an antisemitic campaign that drove about 13,000 Polish Jews to emigrate.

chapters.heading: Easter riots
chapters.text: After the student leader Rudi Dutschke was shot in Berlin on April 11, students blamed the Springer press and blockaded its offices across West Germany. In Munich two people died. Schwabing, the student district, had just been the setting of the year’s comedy hit, Zur Sache, Schätzchen.

chapters.heading: Barricades in the Latin Quarter
chapters.text: Police cleared the occupied Sorbonne on May 3. A week later students built barricades in the Latin Quarter, and by the end of the month around ten million workers were on strike. De Gaulle called an election and won it in June.
chapters.image: Prenez vos désirs pour des réalités - 1968.jpg

chapters.heading: Students against the “red bourgeoisie”
chapters.text: Belgrade students occupied their university for a week, protesting unemployment and the privileges of party officials. Tito went on television and said they were partly right, and the protest ended.

chapters.heading: The tanks arrive
chapters.text: Dubček’s Prague Spring had lifted censorship since January. On the night of August 20, Warsaw Pact armies invaded. Crowds argued with Soviet soldiers on Wenceslas Square, and Marta Kubišová’s “Modlitba pro Martu” became the song of the occupation.

chapters.heading: The stake
chapters.text: Lluís Llach wrote “L’Estaca” in 1968, a song in Catalan about pulling down a rotten stake together, at a time when Franco’s Spain restricted the language. It became an anthem far from Barcelona; in 1978 a Polish version, “Mury,” was taken up by Solidarity.

chapters.heading: Astral Weeks
chapters.text: Northern Ireland’s civil rights marches began that autumn, and students at Queen’s University founded People’s Democracy. In November Van Morrison released Astral Weeks, an album about the Belfast streets he grew up on, months before the city turned violent.

title: Queens
intro: Most of Europe’s thrones passed to sons, so a woman who ruled usually got there by accident, by marriage, or by outliving the men around her.
Each stop is one queen and the room, church, or square where her reign turned. Several of them ended badly.

chapters.heading: Joanna I
chapters.text: Joanna inherited Naples at sixteen. Her first husband, Andrew of Hungary, was strangled in 1345, and many blamed her. She married three more times and ruled for nearly forty years from the Castel Nuovo, until a cousin with Hungarian backing took the city and had her killed in 1382.

chapters.heading: Crowned king
chapters.text: Jadwiga was about ten when she was crowned in Wawel Cathedral, with the title king, since Polish law had no place for a reigning queen. Her marriage to Jogaila of Lithuania joined the two countries for four centuries. She left her jewels to refound Kraków’s university.

chapters.heading: Isabella of Castile
chapters.text: Isabella and her husband Ferdinand held court in Seville’s Alcázar. In the 1480s and 1490s they set up the Spanish Inquisition, finished the conquest of Granada, expelled Spain’s Jews, and paid for Columbus’s first voyage. The trade house that ran the Americas opened in the palace in 1503.
chapters.image: Baths of Maria de Padilla, Alcázar of Seville.jpg

chapters.heading: Hürrem
chapters.text: She was captured as a girl in what is now Ukraine and sold into the harem of Süleyman the Magnificent. He freed and married her, which no sultan had done for centuries, and she became an adviser and a builder. Mimar Sinan designed the bathhouse near Hagia Sophia that carries her name.
chapters.image: İstanbul - Ayasofya Hürrem Sultan Hamamı r3 - Şub 2013.jpg

chapters.heading: Catherine de’ Medici
chapters.text: Catherine was born in the Medici palace in 1519 and orphaned within weeks. At fourteen she was married to the future Henry II of France. After his death she ruled through three of her sons for thirty years of religious war, and was blamed for the St. Bartholomew’s Day massacre of 1572.

chapters.heading: Mary, Queen of Scots
chapters.text: Mary came back from France in 1561 to a Protestant Scotland. In 1566 her secretary David Rizzio was stabbed to death in her supper room at Holyrood, with her husband Darnley among the plotters. A year later Darnley’s house blew up and he was found strangled. She was forced to abdicate that summer.
chapters.image: Palace of Holyroodhouse quadrangle Edinburgh 2025 dllu.jpg

chapters.heading: Christina of Sweden
chapters.text: Christina became queen at six when her father died in battle. She was crowned king in Storkyrkan in 1650, brought Descartes to her court, and refused to marry. In 1654 she gave up the throne, became a Catholic, and moved to Rome, where she is buried in St. Peter’s.

chapters.heading: Caroline Matilda
chapters.text: George III’s sister was married at fifteen to Christian VII of Denmark, who was mentally ill. She and the king’s doctor, Johann Struensee, ran the country together and passed hundreds of reforms. A coup in 1772 ended it. Struensee was executed, and she was divorced and sent away. She died at 23.

chapters.heading: Marie Antoinette
chapters.text: A daughter of Maria Theresa, she was sent from Vienna at fourteen to marry the future Louis XVI. At Versailles she became the face of everything the Revolution hated. After the monarchy fell she spent her last weeks in the Conciergerie prison, and was guillotined in October 1793.

chapters.heading: Sisi
chapters.text: Elisabeth of Bavaria married Franz Joseph at sixteen and never settled at the Viennese court. She traveled constantly, rode, fenced, kept to punishing diets, and was much loved in Hungary. An Italian anarchist stabbed her with a sharpened file on the lakefront in Geneva in 1898.
chapters.image: Schoenbrunn Palace as seen from Neptune Fountain, September 2016.jpg

image: John Opie (1761-1807) - The Murder of Rizzio - 49 - Guildhall Art Gallery.jpg

title: Resistance
intro: Under Nazi rule most people kept their heads down. Some wrote leaflets, hid neighbors, forged papers, or took up guns.
The stops run from Berlin itself to occupied capitals across Europe, ending with the summer and autumn of 1944.

chapters.heading: In the capital
chapters.text: Otto and Elise Hampel, a working couple, spent two years leaving anti-Hitler postcards in Berlin stairwells until they were caught and beheaded in 1943. Hans Fallada turned their story into Alone in Berlin. That same year, women stood for days outside a building on Rosenstraße until the Jewish husbands held inside were released.

chapters.heading: Hunger and the flag
chapters.text: Germany occupied Greece in April 1941, and that winter tens of thousands starved in Athens. In May 1941 two students climbed the Acropolis at night and pulled down the swastika flag. The resistance grew into one of the largest in Europe. On May 1, 1944, the Germans shot 200 prisoners at the Kaisariani firing range.

chapters.place: Warsaw Zoo and the Arsenal, Warsaw
chapters.heading: The zoo and the scouts
chapters.text: Jan Żabiński, director of the Warsaw Zoo, and his wife Antonina hid around 300 Jews over the war in empty animal enclosures and their own villa. In March 1943 Home Army scouts ambushed a Gestapo truck by the old Arsenal to free a captured friend, an action later retold in Stones for the Rampart.

chapters.heading: The White Rose
chapters.text: A handful of Munich students and a professor printed leaflets calling Germans to resist. On February 18, 1943, Hans and Sophie Scholl scattered copies into the university’s atrium from the floor above, and a caretaker saw them. They were tried and beheaded four days later.
chapters.tip: A memorial of bronze leaflets is set into the sidewalk outside the main university building.

chapters.heading: Flame and Citron
chapters.text: Denmark was occupied with a light touch until 1943, when the government resigned and resistance grew. Two young members of the Holger Danske group, known as Flame and Citron, shot informers and collaborators in Copenhagen. Both were dead by October 1944. Executed resistance fighters are buried at Mindelunden in Ryvangen.

chapters.heading: Open city
chapters.text: Germany occupied Rome in September 1943. In March 1944 partisans bombed an SS column on Via Rasella, and the next day the Germans shot 335 men and boys in caves on the Via Ardeatina. Priests hid Jews and escaped prisoners in convents and Vatican buildings. Rossellini filmed Rome, Open City in the same streets in 1945.

chapters.heading: Hiding and fighting
chapters.text: Anne Frank’s family hid behind a bookcase on the Prinsengracht for two years before they were betrayed in August 1944. Others fought: the teenage Oversteegen sisters lured collaborators to be shot, and the banker Walraven van Hall funded the resistance with money taken from the central bank. The Hunger Winter of 1944–45 killed about 20,000.

chapters.heading: Liberation
chapters.text: On August 19, 1944, with Allied armies close, the Paris resistance rose. Fighters took the Hôtel de Ville and Colonel Rol-Tanguy ran the uprising from a bunker under Place Denfert-Rochereau. Hitler ordered the city wrecked. On August 25 the German commander surrendered it intact.
chapters.image: Crowds of French patriots line the Champs Elysees-edit2.jpg

chapters.heading: The last months
chapters.text: Hungary was Germany’s ally until March 1944, when the Germans occupied it and began deporting its Jews. Hannah Szenes, a Budapest-born poet, parachuted in from Palestine with the British and was caught and shot in November. Pinchas Rosenbaum put on a stolen Arrow Cross uniform to pull people out of the deportation lines.
chapters.image: Girl contemplates Shoes on the Danube Bank (Budapest, Hungary).jpg

title: Dictators
intro: Twentieth-century Europe produced dictators of every kind. Some were soldiers, one was a professor, and one was a failed painter.

Most of these men had nothing to do with each other, but their stories have the same shape: a way in, years of control, and an ending. This thread takes them in order, from a men’s hostel in Vienna in 1908 to a square in Bucharest in 1989. Each stop is a place where one regime started or ended.

chapters.heading: Hitler, a failed painter in Vienna
chapters.text: The story starts with a young man who wanted to be a painter. Adolf Hitler moved to Vienna, then the capital of the Austrian empire, hoping to study at its Academy of Fine Arts. The Academy turned him down twice. He stayed anyway, living in cheap lodgings and then in a men’s hostel on Meldemannstraße, a poor street. He got by selling watercolors of the city’s sights. Vienna also gave him his politics. Its mayor, Karl Lueger, won votes by blaming Jews for the city’s problems, and Hitler took note. He left for Munich, in Germany, in 1913. Twenty years later he was running that country.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here show you the Vienna that shaped him.
items: A book describes the city Hitler knew, a place of cheap hostels and resentment.
An audio tour walks you past his lodgings and the academy that rejected him.

chapters.place: Palazzo Venezia, Rome, and Piazzale Loreto, Milan
chapters.heading: Mussolini invents Fascism
chapters.text: Hitler was not the first, though. His model was an Italian. Benito Mussolini was a blacksmith’s son and a former socialist newspaper editor. In 1919 he founded the Fascist movement at a meeting in a hall on Piazza San Sepolcro, a small square in Milan. Three years later he was in power. He ruled from Palazzo Venezia, a palace in the center of Rome, and spoke to crowds from its balcony. The end came from his own side. In July 1943, with the war going badly, his Fascist Grand Council voted him out. In April 1945 he was shot by partisans, the Italian resistance fighters. They hung his body upside down in Piazzale Loreto, a square in Milan.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to follow Mussolini from start to finish.
items: One podcast episode covers his rise, starting with the meeting in Milan.
Another covers his fall in 1943.
A book follows what happened to his body after Piazzale Loreto, which was buried, stolen, and fought over for years.

chapters.heading: Salazar, the professor who ruled Portugal
chapters.text: Not every dictator shouted from a balcony. António de Oliveira Salazar was an economics professor who kept out of the public eye. He ran Portugal for 36 years, from 1932. His secret police, known as the PIDE, did the work that speeches did elsewhere. They held political prisoners in the Aljube, a jail beside Lisbon’s cathedral. Salazar kept Portugal out of the Second World War. Later he fought long wars to hold on to its colonies in Africa. Those wars finished the regime, though he did not live to see it. In April 1974 young army officers, tired of fighting them, overthrew his successors in a single day. People put carnations in the soldiers’ gun barrels. The Aljube is now a museum about the prisoners.

mediaNote.lead: To see what the regime did, and how it ended, there are three things here.
items: A documentary tells the story of the secret police using only prisoners’ mugshots and survivors’ voices.
A feature film re-creates the day of the 1974 coup.
A book covers the same day in more detail.

chapters.heading: Franco and the silence after him
chapters.text: Next door in Spain, the dictator got there by war. Francisco Franco was a general who rose against the elected government in 1936. Three years of civil war followed, and he won in 1939. The killing did not stop with the war. Tens of thousands of people were executed in the years after it, many of them against the wall of the Almudena cemetery in Madrid. Franco ruled until 1975 and died in bed. After his death, Spain agreed not to prosecute the crimes of his regime. The families of the dead are still pushing against that silence.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here go deeper into the killing and the silence.
items: A documentary follows victims of the regime as they go to court decades later.
A long history book counts the civilians killed by Franco’s side.

chapters.heading: Quisling, the name that means traitor
chapters.text: Franco stayed out of Hitler’s war. Norway was not given the choice. Germany invaded in April 1940, and one Norwegian politician had asked for it. Vidkun Quisling had urged Hitler to occupy the country, and on the day of the invasion he announced himself prime minister. From 1942 he led a puppet government, one that took its orders from Berlin. He lived in a villa on Bygdøy, a peninsula on the edge of Oslo, and called it Gimle. After the war he was tried for treason, and he was shot in October 1945. His surname became a word for traitor.

items: For the full story of Quisling, there is a podcast episode about him, and about how his name became an insult.

chapters.heading: Hitler’s last days in the bunker
chapters.text: By then the man Quisling served was already dead. In early 1945 Hitler moved underground, into a bunker beneath the garden of the Reich Chancellery, his headquarters in Berlin. He spent his last weeks there while the Red Army, the army of the Soviet Union, fought its way into the city. Mussolini was shot on April 28. Two days later, on April 30, 1945, Hitler killed himself. The bunker was later demolished. Today the site is a parking lot with a single information board.

mediaNote.lead: There are two ways to get inside the bunker.
items: A short video shows the rooms as they were found, and what became of them.
Downfall is a German feature film about Hitler’s last ten days, based on his secretary’s memoir.

chapters.heading: Tito, who defied Stalin
chapters.text: The war that destroyed Hitler made the next dictator. Josip Broz, known as Tito, led the partisans, the communist fighters who resisted the German occupation of Yugoslavia. In 1945 he took power. Three years later he broke with Joseph Stalin, the Soviet leader, who expected communist countries to obey Moscow. Few people thought Tito would last. He did. He ran Yugoslavia as a one-party state, but one that let its people travel and work abroad. He died in 1980 and is buried in the winter garden of his residence in Belgrade, now called the House of Flowers. About a decade after his death, the country came apart in war.

mediaNote.lead: If Tito interests you, there are three things to try.
items: One podcast episode covers the break with Stalin.
Another covers his death and what followed.
There is also a short biography.

chapters.heading: The colonels who seized Greece
chapters.text: Tito was still in power when soldiers took over the country to his south. On April 21, 1967, a group of Greek army colonels seized the government in a coup, with almost no bloodshed. They banned political parties and censored newspapers, books, and songs. Opponents were jailed and tortured. The challenge came from students. In November 1973 they occupied the Polytechnic, a university in central Athens. The army sent a tank through its gate. The occupation was crushed, but the regime never recovered, and it fell the following summer.

mediaNote.lead: Two short podcast episodes here bring these years closer.
items: In one, a resistance fighter describes the coup and what happened to him afterward.
The other reports on the students at the Polytechnic.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu and the crowd that booed
chapters.text: The last dictator in this thread held on longest. Nicolae Ceaușescu led communist Romania from 1965. Like Tito, he defied Moscow, and in the 1970s Western governments courted him for it. The 1980s were different. He decided to pay off all of Romania’s foreign debt, and his people went hungry while he did it. At the same time he bulldozed a fifth of old Bucharest to build himself a palace. On December 21, 1989, he summoned a crowd to the city’s central square to cheer him. They booed instead. Four days later, on Christmas Day, he and his wife were shot.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways into Ceaușescu’s last decade.
items: A podcast episode covers the speech and the execution.
A short video is about the palace.
In another podcast episode, a British diplomat describes watching Romania go hungry in the early 1980s.

title: Assassinations
intro: Political killings tend to happen in ordinary places: a theater, a church during Mass, a shopping street, a car at a red light. Several of the spots are marked, and a few are still just street corners.
Some of these killings changed what happened next, and some changed very little.

chapters.heading: Caesar
chapters.text: On the Ides of March, senators stabbed Julius Caesar at a meeting in the Theatre of Pompey. They meant to save the Republic, but his death led to civil war and to his adopted son Augustus becoming emperor. The site is now a sunken square with a cat shelter.

chapters.heading: The Pazzi conspiracy
chapters.text: During Sunday Mass in April 1478, men hired by the rival Pazzi family stabbed Giuliano de’ Medici to death in the cathedral. His brother Lorenzo escaped into the sacristy, and the city hunted down the conspirators within days.
chapters.image: Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence Cathedral, interior, 223756.jpg

chapters.heading: Mary’s court
chapters.text: In 1566 Mary, Queen of Scots, watched her secretary David Rizzio stabbed in her supper room at Holyrood. The next year her husband, Lord Darnley, was found dead after the house he was staying in blew up. Within months she had lost her throne.

chapters.heading: A masked ball
chapters.text: King Gustav III was shot in the back at a masked ball in the opera house he had built. He had been warned and went anyway. He died two weeks later.
chapters.image: Kungliga Operan Royal Swedish Opera Stockholm 2016 01.jpg

chapters.heading: The regicide
chapters.text: On February 1, 1908, republican gunmen shot King Carlos I and his heir in their open carriage as it turned out of the Praça do Comércio. Portugal’s monarchy lasted two more years.

chapters.place: Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius, Prague
chapters.heading: Heydrich
chapters.text: Czechoslovak parachutists trained in Britain ambushed Reinhard Heydrich, the Nazi governor of Bohemia, on a bend in a Prague street. He died of his wounds. The parachutists died weeks later in the crypt of a church, and the Nazis destroyed the villages of Lidice and Ležáky in revenge.

chapters.heading: Carrero Blanco
chapters.text: Franco’s prime minister and closest ally, Luis Carrero Blanco, was killed when the Basque group ETA set off a bomb under his car as he left Mass. The blast threw the car over a church building.

chapters.heading: Palme and Lindh
chapters.text: Prime Minister Olof Palme was shot dead in 1986 walking home from the cinema without bodyguards. No one was ever convicted. In 2003 the foreign minister, Anna Lindh, was stabbed while shopping in a department store a short walk away.

chapters.heading: Đinđić
chapters.text: Zoran Đinđić, the prime minister who had sent Slobodan Milošević to the war crimes tribunal in The Hague, was shot by a sniper outside the government building. The killers were tied to a paramilitary unit and organized crime.

chapters.heading: Theo van Gogh
chapters.text: The filmmaker Theo van Gogh was shot and stabbed on an Amsterdam street by a man angered by his short film about Islam and women. A steel sculpture called The Scream stands in the nearby Oosterpark.

image: Vincenzo Camuccini - La morte di Cesare.jpg

title: Heists
intro: Some of the most famous objects in Europe are famous partly because someone took them. Others are still being argued over, two centuries after they were removed.
The thieves here range from a museum handyman to the Nazi leadership to a gang of pensioners.

chapters.heading: The Parthenon sculptures
chapters.text: Around 1801 agents of Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, cut sculptures from the Parthenon and shipped them to Britain. The British Museum has had them since 1816. The Acropolis Museum in Athens, opened in 2009, has a gallery waiting for them.

chapters.heading: The Mona Lisa
chapters.text: In August 1911 Vincenzo Peruggia, who had worked at the Louvre, walked out with the Mona Lisa under his coat. Crowds came to stare at the empty wall. He was caught two years later trying to sell it in Florence, and the painting came home far more famous than it left.

chapters.heading: The Woman in Gold
chapters.text: The Nazis took Klimt’s gold portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer from her family in 1938, and it hung in Vienna’s Belvedere for decades. Her niece Maria Altmann sued Austria and won it back in 2006.

chapters.heading: Göring’s shopping
chapters.text: During the occupation, art seized from Jewish families in France was sorted at the Jeu de Paume in the Tuileries. Hermann Göring came again and again to choose pieces for himself. A curator, Rose Valland, secretly recorded where everything went, which helped return much of it after the war.
chapters.image: Jeu de Paume, Jardin des Tuileries, Paris 25 May 2017.jpg

chapters.heading: The Scream
chapters.text: On the morning the 1994 Winter Olympics opened, two men climbed a ladder into Oslo’s National Gallery, cut The Scream from the wall and left a note thanking it for the poor security. It was recovered three months later. Another version was stolen from the Munch Museum in 2004.
chapters.image: Edvard Munch, The Scream, 1893, National Gallery, Oslo (1) (35658212823).jpg

chapters.heading: The Bührle robbery
chapters.text: In 2008 three armed men walked into a private museum in Zurich and left with four paintings, including a Cézanne and a Van Gogh. All four were eventually found. The collection now hangs in the Kunsthaus.

chapters.heading: The Spider-Man
chapters.text: A burglar known as the Spider-Man cut through a window of the Paris Museum of Modern Art one night in 2010 and took five paintings, including a Picasso and a Matisse. He was caught, but the paintings have never been found.

chapters.heading: Hatton Garden
chapters.text: Over the Easter weekend of 2015 a gang of men mostly in their sixties and seventies drilled through the wall of a safe-deposit vault in London’s jewelry quarter. They were caught within weeks, partly because they talked about it in their cars.

image: Visitors of Louvre in front of Mona Lisa.jpg

title: Organized crime
intro: Port cities and poor housing projects have bred gangs everywhere, but some have shaped how their cities are seen: Marseille and heroin, Naples and the Camorra, Belgrade’s gangster-celebrities of the 1990s.
Most of the stories here are told by journalists who paid for it, or by films the cities have mixed feelings about.

chapters.heading: Carbone and Spirito
chapters.text: Paul Carbone and François Spirito ran protection, gambling, and prostitution in interwar Marseille, with friends in city politics. Borsalino, with Alain Delon and Jean-Paul Belmondo, is loosely based on them.

chapters.heading: The French Connection
chapters.text: Corsican gangs in Marseille refined heroin and shipped it to New York until the network was broken up in the early 1970s. A judge who went after its successors, Pierre Michel, was shot dead in 1981. Today street gangs fight over drug dealing in the northern estates.

chapters.heading: The Special Unit
chapters.text: In 1973 Glasgow’s Barlinnie Prison opened a unit that gave its most violent long-term prisoners art materials and a say in how it was run. Its best-known inmate, the gangster Jimmy Boyle, came out a sculptor and writer.

chapters.heading: The Magliana gang
chapters.text: The Banda della Magliana, named after a district in the south of Rome, ran much of the city’s drug trade and gambling, and was tied to neo-fascists, the secret services, and the Vatican bank scandal.

chapters.heading: The Long Good Friday
chapters.text: In The Long Good Friday Bob Hoskins plays a London gang boss who wants to redevelop the derelict docks as the old East End world falls apart around him. A few years later the docks really were redeveloped.
chapters.image: East Dock. St Katharine Docks, London 02.jpg

chapters.heading: The Camorra
chapters.text: The Camorra shot the young reporter Giancarlo Siani in 1985 for writing about it. In 2006 Roberto Saviano’s book Gomorrah named the clans and their business, from fake couture to toxic waste, and he has lived under police protection since. The Vele towers of Scampia, where the clan wars were fought, are being demolished.

chapters.heading: A bomb at the Uffizi
chapters.text: In May 1993 the Sicilian Mafia set off a car bomb in the narrow street behind the Uffizi, part of a campaign against the Italian state. Five people died, and paintings in the gallery were damaged.

chapters.heading: Belgrade’s lost decade
chapters.text: During the wars and sanctions of the 1990s, smugglers and paramilitaries became rich and famous in Belgrade, appearing in magazines and marrying pop stars. The film The Wounds follows two boys from New Belgrade who want to be them.

chapters.heading: Veronica Guerin
chapters.text: The journalist Veronica Guerin was shot at a red light in 1996 after years of writing about Dublin’s drug gangs. Within months Ireland set up the Criminal Assets Bureau to seize criminals’ money.

title: Heretics and witches
intro: For four centuries, believing the wrong thing could get you burned. Churches, both Catholic and Protestant, and the states behind them tried and killed reformers, scientists, alleged witches, and anyone who read the wrong book.
The stops follow it from Jan Hus to the end of the Spanish Inquisition.

chapters.heading: Jan Hus
chapters.text: Jan Hus preached church reform in Czech at the Bethlehem Chapel. He was summoned to the Council of Constance under a promise of safe conduct, then tried and burned as a heretic in 1415. His followers held off five crusades in the Hussite Wars that followed.

chapters.heading: The Inquisition begins
chapters.text: The Spanish Inquisition held its first auto-da-fé in Seville in 1481 and kept its headquarters in the Castillo de San Jorge in Triana for three centuries. Its first targets were Jews who had converted to Christianity. Around 1560 it burned a group of Seville monks who had been translating the Bible into Spanish.
chapters.tip: The castle’s ruins are now a small museum under the Triana market.

chapters.heading: Savonarola
chapters.text: The friar Girolamo Savonarola ran Florence for four years on sermons against luxury. In February 1497 his followers burned mirrors, cards, books, and paintings in a bonfire in Piazza della Signoria. A year later he was excommunicated, tortured, and burned in the same square.
chapters.image: Savonarola's execution memorial, Piazza della Signoria, Florence (26073214863).jpg

chapters.heading: Veronica Franco
chapters.text: Veronica Franco was a courtesan and a published poet in Venice. In 1580 she was brought before the Inquisition on a charge of witchcraft. She defended herself and was acquitted, probably helped by her friends among the city’s nobility.

chapters.heading: Scotland’s witch trials
chapters.text: Scotland tried several thousand people for witchcraft, most of them women. The panic began in 1590 when James VI blamed witches for storms that nearly sank his ship. Hundreds of the accused were strangled and burned on Castlehill, by the castle. A small fountain there, the Witches’ Well, remembers them.

chapters.heading: Giordano Bruno
chapters.text: The former friar Giordano Bruno argued that the universe was infinite and full of other worlds. After eight years of trial he refused to recant, and on February 17, 1600, he was burned alive in Campo de’ Fiori. A hooded statue of him has stood over the market since 1889.
chapters.image: Statue of Giordano Bruno, Campo de' Fiori (45788557464).jpg

chapters.heading: Galileo
chapters.text: In 1633 the Inquisition in Rome found Galileo vehemently suspected of heresy for teaching that the earth moves around the sun. He was made to recant on his knees and spent his last nine years under house arrest in a villa at Arcetri, above Florence, still working.

chapters.place: Plaza Mayor and the Prado, Madrid
chapters.heading: The last trials
chapters.text: The grandest auto-da-fé was held in Madrid’s Plaza Mayor in 1680 before the king. By Goya’s time the Inquisition was weaker but still dangerous; he was questioned over his Naked Maja. Napoleon abolished it in 1808, the restored king brought it back, and it was finally ended in 1834.

image: Pedro Berruguete - Saint Dominic Presiding over an Auto-da-fe (detail) - c. 1491-1499 - 02.jpg

title: The Roman Empire
intro: At its height Rome ruled from Scotland to Syria, and it left roads, walls, theaters, and towns across Europe that later cities were built on top of. Plenty of it is underground, in basements, under squares, and under office buildings.
Rome itself comes first, then the provinces, and finally the people who left when the empire fell apart.

chapters.place: Ara Pacis and the Forum, Rome
chapters.heading: Augustus
chapters.text: Caesar’s adopted son Augustus ended the civil wars, called himself first citizen rather than king, and ruled for forty years. The Senate built him the Altar of Peace, and his statue from his wife’s villa shows him as a young general.

chapters.heading: Londinium
chapters.text: The Romans founded Londinium by a bridge over the Thames around 47. Boudica’s rebels burned it in 60 or 61, leaving a red layer archaeologists still find. A temple to Mithras now sits under an office building, and stretches of the wall survive by Tower Hill.
chapters.image: London Roman Wall - surviving section by Tower Hill gardens full section.jpg

chapters.heading: Pompeii
chapters.text: Pompeii is the best picture we have of an ordinary Roman town: its bakeries, bars, graffiti, and election slogans, all frozen by the eruption of 79.

chapters.heading: Emperors from Spain
chapters.text: Itálica, outside Seville, was founded for Roman veterans in 206 BC. Trajan, born there, became the first emperor from outside Italy, and his successor Hadrian came from a family there. Hadrian later rebuilt the Pantheon in Rome.
chapters.image: Anfiteatro de las ruinas romanas de Itálica, Santiponce, Sevilla, España, 2015-12-06, DD 34-45 PAN HDR.JPG

chapters.heading: Olisipo
chapters.text: Roman Lisbon, Olisipo, had a theater on the hillside below the castle. Its remains were found under houses in the 1790s, after the earthquake.

chapters.heading: Singidunum
chapters.text: Belgrade began as Singidunum, a legion’s fortress on the Danube frontier. One of the city’s main streets still follows the Roman road out of the camp.

chapters.heading: Capital of the West
chapters.text: For about a century Milan was the capital of the western half of the empire. In 313 Constantine and his co-emperor agreed there to tolerate Christianity, and the bishop Ambrose later founded the church where he is buried.

chapters.heading: Constantine
chapters.text: After winning Rome at the Milvian Bridge, Constantine got a triumphal arch beside the Colosseum, decorated partly with reliefs taken from older monuments. He went on to found a new capital at Constantinople.

chapters.heading: After Rome
chapters.text: As the empire collapsed, people from mainland towns fled to the islands of the lagoon. Refugees from Altinum settled Torcello, using stone from the old Roman towns, and their settlements grew into Venice.
chapters.image: Venedig Torcello Basilica di Santa Maria Assunta-4345.jpg

image: Colosseum and Arch of Constantine seen from Palatine.jpg

title: Byzantium
intro: The Roman Empire carried on in the east for a thousand years after Rome fell, ruled from Constantinople. The Byzantines called themselves Romans, and their capital was the richest city in Christendom.
Much of what survives was taken elsewhere. This thread starts in the city and follows the loot.

chapters.heading: Hagia Sophia
chapters.text: Justinian’s Hagia Sophia, finished in 537, had the largest dome in the world for nearly a thousand years. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020. Its mosaics are still visible upstairs.

chapters.heading: The walls
chapters.text: Three lines of land walls, built in the 400s, kept Constantinople safe for a thousand years. Most of their six kilometers still stand.

chapters.heading: The Fourth Crusade
chapters.text: In 1204 a crusader army meant for Egypt turned on Constantinople instead, sacked it, and put a Latin emperor on its throne. Venice, which had built the fleet, took a large share of the loot.
chapters.image: The Entry of the Crusaders into Constantinople - 1840 - Eugène Delacroix - Louvre - Inv 3821.jpg

chapters.heading: The loot in Venice
chapters.text: The four bronze horses over St. Mark’s came from Constantinople’s Hippodrome, and the porphyry Tetrarchs set into the basilica’s corner were taken from the city too. Venice built its sea empire partly on what it took.
chapters.image: Horses of Basilica San Marco bright.jpg

chapters.heading: The Barberini Ivory
chapters.text: An ivory panel of an emperor on horseback, made in Constantinople in the 500s, passed through a Roman cardinal’s collection to the Louvre.

chapters.heading: The Archangel Michael
chapters.text: The largest Byzantine ivory panel to survive, an archangel holding a scepter and orb, is in the British Museum.

title: Vikings
intro: For about three centuries, Scandinavians raided, traded, and settled from Ireland to the Black Sea. Several of today’s capitals began as their towns or were shaped by them.
The stops follow them from their homelands westward.

chapters.heading: At home
chapters.text: Most Vikings were farmers, and raiding was a summer occupation. Denmark’s National Museum holds much of what survives of daily life, from weapons to jewelry.

chapters.heading: East to Byzantium
chapters.text: Swedish Vikings mostly went east, along the rivers of Russia to Constantinople and Baghdad. Silver coins from the Islamic world turn up in Swedish graves by the tens of thousands.

chapters.place: Museum of the Viking Age, Oslo
chapters.heading: The Oseberg ship
chapters.text: In 834, two women were buried in a ship at Oseberg, south of Oslo, with sledges, a cart, and animals. The ship survived in the clay for eleven centuries and is now in Oslo’s Viking museum, which is being rebuilt around it.

chapters.heading: Dyflin
chapters.text: Vikings set up a fortified camp on the Liffey in 841, and it grew into a trading town. In the 1970s Dublin built its civic offices on top of the excavated Viking town at Wood Quay, despite large protests.

chapters.heading: Iceland
chapters.text: Norse settlers reached Iceland around 870. The sagas say the first, Ingólfur Arnarson, threw his high-seat pillars overboard and settled where they washed up: Reykjavík. A longhouse from the period is under a hotel on Aðalstræti.

title: The Habsburgs
intro: For four hundred years one family married and inherited its way into ruling much of Europe, from Spain and the Netherlands to Bohemia and Hungary. Its palaces, crypts, and art collections are still among the main sights in half a dozen cities.
The thread follows the family west to east and through to its end in 1918.

chapters.heading: Charles V
chapters.text: Charles V was born in Ghent and came of age in Brussels, ruling the Netherlands, Spain, its American colonies, and the Holy Roman Empire. In 1555, worn out, he gave up his thrones in the great hall of the Coudenberg Palace in Brussels. Its remains are under the Place Royale.
chapters.image: Brussels, straatzicht Place Royale met église Saint-Jacques-sur-Coudenberg oeg2043-01020 en standbeeld van Godefroid de Bouillon foto3 2015-06-07 13.53.jpg

chapters.heading: The Spanish branch
chapters.text: Charles’s son Philip II made Madrid the capital of Spain. The Spanish Habsburgs collected the paintings that became the Prado. In Las Meninas, Velázquez painted the court of Philip IV around the king’s young daughter. The line ended in 1700 with Charles II, who had no children.

chapters.heading: Rudolf’s court
chapters.text: Emperor Rudolf II moved his court to Prague and filled the castle with astronomers, alchemists, and art. Tycho Brahe worked for him. In 1618 Protestant nobles threw two imperial governors and their secretary out of a castle window, and the Thirty Years’ War began.

chapters.heading: The imperial capital
chapters.text: After the Ottoman siege of 1683, Vienna grew into the imperial capital: the Hofburg in town, Schönbrunn as the summer palace, and the Kunsthistorisches Museum for the collections. Franz Joseph reigned for 68 years, from 1848 to 1916, and his wife Elisabeth, Sisi, became a legend.
chapters.image: Hofburg Neue Burg section, Heldenplatz. Statue of Archduke Charles.jpg

chapters.heading: Austria-Hungary
chapters.text: After losing a war to Prussia, Franz Joseph agreed in 1867 to share power with Hungary: two countries under one monarch. Budapest boomed, building its parliament, opera, and boulevards to rival Vienna.

chapters.heading: The end
chapters.text: Franz Joseph’s only son, Rudolf, died with his young lover at Mayerling in 1889. His nephew and heir, Franz Ferdinand, was shot in Sarajevo in 1914, and the war that followed ended the empire in 1918. The family is buried in the Capuchin Crypt in Vienna.

title: The Ottoman frontier
intro: For more than three centuries the Ottoman Empire pushed into Europe and Europe pushed back. The frontier ran through cities that changed hands, held sieges, and still carry the marks.
The stops run in date order, from the fall of Constantinople to Greek independence.

chapters.heading: Constantinople falls
chapters.text: Mehmed II’s cannons broke the thousand-year-old land walls of Constantinople in May 1453. He made the city his capital and built the Topkapı Palace above the Bosphorus.

chapters.heading: The gate to Hungary
chapters.text: In 1456 John Hunyadi held Belgrade’s fortress against Mehmed II; church bells still ring at noon in memory of the victory. In 1521 Suleiman the Magnificent took it.

chapters.heading: Vlad the Impaler
chapters.text: Vlad III of Wallachia, who fought the Ottomans with notorious cruelty, is the first ruler known to have signed a document in Bucharest. His court’s ruins are in the Old Town.

chapters.heading: Ottoman Buda
chapters.text: The Ottomans held Buda for 145 years. They left Turkish baths that are still in use, and the tomb of the dervish Gül Baba, which is still a place of pilgrimage.
chapters.image: Rudas Baths central part and Gellert Hill in Tabán, 2016 Budapest.jpg

chapters.place: Arsenale and the Grand Canal, Venice
chapters.heading: Lepanto
chapters.text: Venice traded with the Ottomans and fought them. Its Arsenale built much of the Christian fleet that sank the Ottoman navy at Lepanto in 1571. Turkish merchants had their own trading house on the Grand Canal, the Fondaco dei Turchi.
chapters.image: (Venice) Battaglia di Lepanto - Andrea Vicentino - Correr Museum.jpg

chapters.heading: The second siege
chapters.text: In 1683 an Ottoman army besieged Vienna for two months. On September 12 a relief army under the Polish king Jan III Sobieski charged down from the Kahlenberg and broke it.

chapters.heading: Sobieski’s palace
chapters.text: Jan III Sobieski came home a hero and built Wilanów as his summer palace, decorated with scenes of his victories.

chapters.heading: The Parthenon explodes
chapters.text: In 1687 a Venetian shell hit Ottoman gunpowder stored in the Parthenon and blew out its middle. In 1821 the Greeks rose against Ottoman rule, and Athens became the capital of an independent Greece in 1834.

image: Relief of Vienna 1683 - Wien Museum - 2 (photo by Andrew Nash).jpg

title: Napoleon
intro: Napoleon Bonaparte rose from an artillery officer to emperor of the French in less than ten years. By 1810 he controlled most of continental Europe, and the cities he took still show the marks.
This thread follows his rise and fall, from a street fight in Paris to the battlefield at Waterloo, and ends at his tomb under a golden dome.

chapters.heading: A whiff of grapeshot
chapters.text: Napoleon was born in 1769 on Corsica, an island in the Mediterranean that had become French only the year before. He trained as an artillery officer in France, and the French Revolution, which began in 1789, gave ambitious young officers fast promotion. In October 1795, royalist crowds marched on the revolutionary government in Paris. The government put the 26-year-old Bonaparte in charge of its guns. He brought up cannon and fired on the rebels near the church of Saint-Roch, on the Rue Saint-Honoré, killing hundreds. The historian Thomas Carlyle later called it “a whiff of grapeshot.” It made Bonaparte’s name, and within months he had command of an army in Italy.

items: To hear what happened that day, there is a podcast episode about the fight outside the church.

chapters.heading: The end of a republic
chapters.text: In Italy he beat the Austrians again and again, and in 1797 his army reached the edge of the Venetian lagoon. Venice had been an independent republic for about eleven hundred years, ruled by elected doges and a Great Council of noble families. Its power had come from trade, and from the Arsenale, the vast state shipyard that was said to build a war galley in a day. By 1797 it had little left to fight with. On May 12 the Great Council voted to dissolve the republic. Napoleon then handed Venice to Austria in a peace treaty, and his soldiers took the four bronze horses from the front of St. Mark’s Basilica to Paris.

items: If you want the longer story, a historian of Venice explains how the city grew rich on its navy, and how Napoleon brought it down.

chapters.heading: The picture of power
chapters.text: Napoleon understood that power depended on pictures. In 1799 he seized control of the French government, and the next year he led an army across the Alps into Italy. He made the crossing on a mule, led by a local guide. But he asked the painter Jacques-Louis David to show him calm on a fiery horse, and David painted a rearing stallion against a stormy sky, in five versions. The first hangs at Malmaison, the country house west of Paris that Napoleon shared with his wife, Josephine. Another painter, Antoine-Jean Gros, showed him touching plague victims in Jaffa, in Palestine, to answer reports that he had left his sick soldiers to die. In 1804, in Notre-Dame, he crowned himself emperor.

mediaNote.lead: Two of the paintings made for him are worth a closer look.
items: A video from Great Art Explained shows how David’s portrait was made as propaganda.
A shorter one looks at Gros’s picture of the plague hospital, which now hangs in the Louvre.

chapters.heading: King of Italy
chapters.text: In 1805 he took a second crown. In Milan Cathedral he crowned himself King of Italy, using the old Iron Crown of the Lombard kings. His government closed many churches and monasteries across northern Italy and took their paintings. The best were gathered in Milan, in the Brera palace, where they became one of Italy’s great galleries, the Pinacoteca di Brera. Among them is a painting by Tintoretto, brought from Venice, of the body of Saint Mark being found in Alexandria. Other pictures went to the Louvre in Paris, which was then called the Musée Napoléon. Many came back after his fall, but some never did, among them a Titian taken from a church in Milan.
chapters.image: Pinacoteca di Brera - Milano - il cortile interno.JPG

mediaNote.lead: Here are two of the paintings his armies moved.
items: A video looks at Tintoretto’s Finding of the Body of Saint Mark, with men pulling bodies from tombs in a long, dark hall.
Another looks at Titian’s Crowning with Thorns, the painting from Milan that is still in the Louvre.

chapters.heading: The second and third of May
chapters.text: Spain was next. In 1808 he forced the Spanish king to give up the throne and made his own brother Joseph king instead. French troops were already in Madrid, and on May 2 the people of the city rose against them, fighting with knives and stones. The French crushed the rising, and that night and the next morning they shot hundreds of prisoners on the hills outside the city. The war that followed lasted six years. When it was over, in 1814, Francisco Goya, the Spanish court painter, painted both days. His Third of May, with a man in a white shirt raising his arms before a firing squad, hangs in the Prado.
chapters.image: El Tres de Mayo, by Francisco de Goya, from Prado (cropped).jpg

mediaNote.lead: If you are going to the Prado, two things will help.
items: A video explains how Goya’s painting works, and why it has shaped how artists show war.
A costume drama by Miloš Forman follows Goya through the years of the Inquisition and the French invasion, though it is uneven.

chapters.heading: The Congress of Vienna
chapters.text: The Spanish war drained his armies, and in 1812 he lost most of what was left in Russia. Vienna knew him well. His troops had occupied the city twice, and in 1810 he married Marie Louise, the daughter of the Austrian emperor. In 1814 he was beaten and sent into exile on Elba, an island off the Italian coast. The rulers of Europe then met in Vienna to decide what to do with the continent. For nine months, Prince Metternich, the Austrian foreign minister, ran the talks from his office on the Ballhausplatz, while the court kept the visitors busy with balls and banquets. One guest joked that the congress danced a great deal but did not move forward.

items: To understand what was decided there, there is a podcast episode about the diplomats who redrew the map of Europe between banquets and balls.

chapters.heading: Waterloo
chapters.text: While they were still talking, Napoleon escaped from Elba. In March 1815 he landed in the south of France, marched to Paris, and took back power without a fight. He ruled for about a hundred days. The allied armies gathered in Belgium, and on June 18 he attacked a British-led army under the Duke of Wellington near the village of Waterloo, south of Brussels. The fighting lasted all day. In the evening a Prussian army under Marshal Blücher arrived, and the French broke and ran. Napoleon was sent to Saint Helena, a tiny British island in the South Atlantic. A tall mound topped by an iron lion now marks the battlefield.
chapters.image: Belgique Butte du Lion dit de Waterloo.jpg

items: For the battle itself, there is a podcast episode in which Dan Snow and his father, Peter Snow, go through the day.

chapters.heading: Back to Paris
chapters.text: He died on Saint Helena in 1821, at 51. By then the French had begun to remember him more kindly, as the general who had made France great, and in 1840 the king, Louis-Philippe, asked the British to return his body. It was carried up the Seine and through Paris in a huge procession. It now lies in a tomb of red stone under the golden dome of Les Invalides, a hospital for old soldiers built by Louis XIV. Other traces of him are all over the city. The column on Place Vendôme is covered in bronze from captured cannon, and the Arc de Triomphe celebrates his victories.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways to see Napoleon’s Paris.
items: A short video at his tomb tells the story of his rise and fall.
A walking tour starts at the Arc de Triomphe du Carrousel, passes the column on Place Vendôme, and ends at the tomb.

title: Ships and harbors
intro: For most of history the richest cities were the ones with the best harbors. Ships brought settlers, trade, and emigrants, and building them employed whole districts.
Most of the old shipyards have closed. Several have been turned into museums, hotels, or apartments.

chapters.heading: A Greek harbor
chapters.text: Greek sailors from Phocaea founded Massalia around a natural harbor in about 600 BC, making Marseille France’s oldest city. Fishermen still sell their catch straight off the boats on the quay.

chapters.heading: The Arsenale
chapters.text: Venice built its war fleets in the Arsenale, a walled state shipyard where thousands worked. Ships moved past a line of workshops as they were fitted out, and at its height it was said to turn out a galley in a day.

chapters.heading: Setting out
chapters.text: Vasco da Gama sailed from Belém in 1497 and reached India by sea. The Jerónimos Monastery was built with the profits of the spice trade, and he is buried there.
chapters.image: Monument of the Discoveries in Belém, Lisbon, 20250604 1030 9078.jpg

chapters.heading: Gateway to the Americas
chapters.text: For two centuries every legal ship between Spain and the Americas had to pass through Seville, 80 kilometers up the Guadalquivir. The Torre del Oro guarded the river port. When the river silted up, the trade moved to Cádiz.

chapters.heading: Famine ships
chapters.text: During the Great Famine, hundreds of thousands left from Dublin’s quays for Liverpool and America. A replica emigrant ship, the Jeanie Johnston, is moored on the Liffey.

chapters.heading: The Pier Head
chapters.text: Herman Melville came to Liverpool as a young sailor in 1839 and found its docks full of emigrant ships. By 1900 the great liners sailed from the Pier Head. The Lusitania was heading home here when a U-boat sank her in 1915.
chapters.image: "The Three Graces", Liverpool Pier Head - geograph.org.uk - 4866613.jpg

chapters.heading: Titanic
chapters.text: Harland & Wolff built the Titanic and her sister ships on slipways on Queen’s Island. Her designer, Thomas Andrews, went down with her. The drawing offices are now a hotel, and the slipways sit beside the Titanic museum.

chapters.heading: Clydebuilt
chapters.text: At one point the Clyde built about a fifth of the world’s ships. In 1883 the steamer Daphne capsized at her launch with 124 workers aboard. The QE2 was the last great liner built there, and in 1971 the workers of Upper Clyde Shipbuilders refused to let the yards close.

chapters.heading: The Cod Wars
chapters.text: Iceland lives on fish, and it pushed its fishing limits from 4 miles out to 200. When British trawlers kept fishing, Icelandic coastguard ships cut their nets, and the Royal Navy came to protect them. Iceland won.
chapters.image: Elding Whale Watching boats Reykjavik harbour (25381979881).jpg

image: Finnieston Crane ^ Clyde Arc Bridge - geograph.org.uk - 3851383.jpg

title: Going underground
intro: London opened the first underground railway in 1863, with steam engines in shallow tunnels. Budapest and Glasgow followed, then Paris, and by the end of the twentieth century almost every big European city had one.
This thread rides through some of the oldest and strangest of them.

chapters.heading: The first
chapters.text: The Metropolitan Railway opened in January 1863 between Paddington and Farringdon, through Edgware Road and Baker Street. Steam trains ran in shallow trenches roofed over under the street. Some stations later closed and are now used for filming.

chapters.heading: The first on the Continent
chapters.text: Budapest opened the first underground railway in continental Europe in 1896, for the celebration of Hungary’s thousandth year. Its little yellow trains still run just under Andrássy Avenue to Heroes’ Square.

chapters.heading: The Clockwork Orange
chapters.text: Glasgow’s subway opened at the end of 1896, the third in the world. It is still one loop of fifteen stations under both banks of the Clyde, with trains so small they are known as the Clockwork Orange.
chapters.image: Subway train at Buchanan Street, Glasgow - DSC06203.JPG

chapters.heading: The Métro
chapters.text: Paris argued for decades about whether its railway should run above or below the street. The first Métro line opened underground in July 1900, in time for the World’s Fair, with Hector Guimard’s green iron entrances.
chapters.image: Travaux du métro. Station gare de Lyon, vue prise en bas, 12ème arrondissement, Paris. 6 avril 1900. PH16949.jpg

chapters.heading: Spain goes underground
chapters.text: Madrid’s first line opened in 1919. Its Chamberí station closed in 1966 when platforms had to be lengthened, and it is now a museum you see from passing trains. Barcelona followed in 1924 with a line from Plaça de Catalunya.

chapters.heading: Painted caves
chapters.text: Stockholm’s tunnelbana opened in 1950. Many stations were blasted into bedrock and left rough, then painted by artists, and parts of the system were built to double as shelters in a nuclear war.

chapters.heading: Digging through history
chapters.text: New lines in old cities turn into archaeology. In Istanbul, digging for the Marmaray tunnel uncovered a Byzantine harbor with dozens of wrecked ships. In Rome, the stations of Metro C near the Colosseum display what was found on the way down.
chapters.image: Roma Colosseo Metro C Fori Imperiali.jpg

chapters.heading: No metro yet
chapters.text: Belgrade has planned a metro since the 1920s and is one of the biggest cities in Europe without one. The closest thing is Vukov Spomenik, a deep station on the city railway that opened in 1995.

image: Kungsträdgården T-bana Metro station in Stockholm Sweden.png

title: Art Nouveau
intro: Around 1900, architects and designers in a dozen cities turned against historical styles and tried something new: curving iron, plant forms, tiles, glass, and furniture designed to match the building. It had a different name nearly everywhere it went: Art Nouveau, Modernisme, Secession, Jugendstil, Liberty.
It lasted about twenty years, until the First World War, and much of it is still standing.

chapters.heading: Where it began
chapters.text: Victor Horta’s Hôtel Tassel, a townhouse for a professor, is usually called the first Art Nouveau building: iron columns that branch like stems, and lines painted on the walls that carry on the curves. Horta’s own house and studio nearby is now his museum.

chapters.place: Glasgow School of Art and Sauchiehall Street, Glasgow
chapters.heading: Mackintosh’s Glasgow
chapters.text: Charles Rennie Mackintosh designed the Glasgow School of Art and, with Margaret Macdonald, the Willow Tea Rooms for Kate Cranston, down to the chairs and cutlery. The art school burned in 2014 and again in 2018. The tea rooms have been restored and serve tea again.

chapters.heading: The Métro entrances
chapters.text: For the new Métro, Hector Guimard designed cast-iron entrances that look like plants growing out of the sidewalk. Parisians called the whole style “style Métro.” Porte Dauphine and Abbesses keep the rare versions with glass canopies.

chapters.heading: Modernisme
chapters.text: In Barcelona the style became Modernisme and a statement of Catalan identity. On one block of Passeig de Gràcia, rival architects built houses side by side, including Gaudí’s Casa Batlló. Lluís Domènech i Montaner’s Palau de la Música, all glass and mosaic, opened in 1908.

chapters.heading: Liberty
chapters.text: Italians called it stile Liberty, after the London shop that sold the new designs. Milan’s wealthiest examples are around Porta Venezia, including Palazzo Castiglioni, whose stone nudes over the door upset the neighbors enough that they were moved.
chapters.image: 9028 - Milano, C.so Venezia - Giuseppe Sommaruga, Pal. Castiglioni (1904) - Foto Giovanni Dall'Orto 22-Apr-2007.jpg

chapters.heading: The Secession
chapters.text: In 1897 Gustav Klimt and other artists left Vienna’s official academy and built their own exhibition hall, with a dome of gilded laurel leaves and the motto “To every age its art, to art its freedom.” Klimt’s Beethoven Frieze is in its basement. The Kiss, from 1908, is at the Belvedere.

chapters.heading: Mucha comes home
chapters.text: Alphonse Mucha made his name in Paris with posters of Sarah Bernhardt. Back in Prague he decorated the Lord Mayor’s Hall in the Municipal House, the city’s showpiece concert hall and café, finished in 1912. Two years later the war ended the style almost everywhere.
chapters.image: Casa municipal, Praga, República Checa, 2022-07-02, DD 09.jpg

title: World’s fairs
intro: For a century, cities staged world’s fairs to show off: new technology, new architecture, and themselves. Many of the buildings were meant to be temporary, and some of the best known are still standing.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: Barcelona’s first fair
chapters.text: Barcelona held a universal exhibition in 1888 on the site of a hated military citadel, which became Ciutadella Park. Eduardo Mendoza’s novel City of Marvels is set in the city that grew around it.

chapters.heading: Paris three times
chapters.text: Paris built the Eiffel Tower as the entrance to the 1889 fair, and it was meant to come down after twenty years. The 1900 fair brought the first Métro line. At the 1937 fair the Soviet and German pavilions faced each other, and Picasso’s Guernica hung in the Spanish one.
chapters.image: Eiffel tower at Exposition Universelle, Paris, 1889.jpg

chapters.heading: The Ibero-American Exposition
chapters.text: Seville’s 1929 fair was for Spain and its former American colonies. Its centrepiece, the semicircular Plaza de España with a tiled bench for every province, is now one of the city’s best-known sights.

chapters.heading: Mies’s pavilion
