chapters.text: For the 1929 fair on Montjuïc, Mies van der Rohe built the German pavilion: marble, glass, steel, and almost nothing else. It was taken down after the fair and rebuilt on the same site in 1986.

chapters.heading: The Empire Exhibition
chapters.text: Glasgow’s 1938 Empire Exhibition filled Bellahouston Park with modernist pavilions and a 90-meter tower. Twelve million people came. Little of it was kept.
chapters.image: 1938 Empire Exhibition view west along Scottish Avenue.jpg

chapters.heading: The fair that never opened
chapters.text: Mussolini planned a world’s fair for 1942 to mark twenty years of Fascism, and began a new district south of Rome for it. The war stopped it, and the district, EUR, was finished after the war.
chapters.image: Palazzo della civiltà del lavoro (EUR, Rome) (5904657870).jpg

chapters.heading: The Atomium
chapters.text: Brussels’ 1958 fair, the first after the war, was about the peaceful atom. Its symbol, a 102-meter model of an iron crystal, was supposed to be dismantled afterward and is still there.

chapters.heading: Feeding the planet
chapters.text: Milan’s Expo 2015 was about food. The site, outside the city at Rho, is being turned into a science and research district.

title: Socialist cities
intro: Socialist governments wanted to build new kinds of cities: workers’ housing with courtyards and kindergartens, wide avenues for parades, towers to show who was in charge. Red Vienna did it by vote in the 1920s. After 1945 the communist states did it on a much bigger scale.
This thread follows the buildings, from public housing to Ceaușescu’s palace.

chapters.heading: Red Vienna
chapters.text: Vienna’s Social Democrats built tens of thousands of public apartments in the 1920s, paid for by new taxes on luxuries. The Karl-Marx-Hof is a kilometer long, with laundries, baths, and kindergartens. The city still owns its apartments and still builds more.

chapters.heading: A steel town for Kraków
chapters.text: Poland’s communist government built Nowa Huta from 1949 next to Kraków: a huge steelworks and a planned town for its workers, partly to outweigh the old Catholic university city. Its avenues radiate from a central square. Wajda’s Man of Marble is about one of the bricklayers who built it.
chapters.image: Nowa Huta - Plac Centralny z lotu ptaka.jpg

chapters.place: Palace of Culture and Science, Warsaw
chapters.heading: Stalin’s gift
chapters.text: Warsaw was rebuilt in the Soviet style called socialist realism: the MDM district has arcades and reliefs of model workers. Then the Soviet Union built the Palace of Culture and Science as a gift from Stalin. Many Varsovians still dislike it, but the Rolling Stones played there in 1967.
chapters.image: Palace of Culture and Science, Warsaw (by Pudelek).jpg

chapters.heading: Stalinallee to Plattenbau
chapters.text: East Berlin built a grand boulevard of tiled apartment blocks, Stalinallee, and the building workers there started the uprising of June 1953. It was renamed Karl-Marx-Allee in 1961. Later, East Germany switched to cheaper prefabricated blocks, Plattenbau, and put up hundreds of thousands of apartments.
chapters.image: Berlin-Friedrichshain, zicht op de Karl Marx Allee bij de Friedrichs Strasse Dm09085173 IMG 5358 2024-09-05 09.28.jpg

chapters.heading: New Belgrade
chapters.text: After 1948 Tito’s Yugoslavia built a new capital on marshland across the Sava: government buildings, huge housing blocks, and the twin towers of the Western City Gate. Yugoslavia had broken with Stalin in 1948, and its architects followed Western modernism rather than Soviet models.

chapters.heading: A tower over Žižkov
chapters.text: Communist Czechoslovakia began a television tower in the old working-class district of Žižkov in 1985. Many people believed it was also meant to jam Western broadcasts. It was finished after the regime fell. In 2000 the artist David Černý added giant crawling babies to its sides.

chapters.heading: Ceaușescu’s palace
chapters.text: Nicolae Ceaușescu had a fifth of old Bucharest demolished, churches and all, to make room for a palace and a boulevard longer than the Champs-Élysées. Romanians lived with food and power shortages while it went up. It was unfinished when he was overthrown in 1989.
chapters.image: Palace of the Parliament in Bucharest (51878975552).jpg

title: Cathedrals
intro: A great cathedral could take centuries to build, outlive the people who started it, and end up in a style they would not have recognized.
Each stop is one church and how it got built.

chapters.heading: Hagia Sophia
chapters.text: After riots burned the old church in 532, the emperor Justinian had Hagia Sophia rebuilt in under six years, with a dome that seemed to float. It was the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years. It became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

chapters.heading: St. Mark’s
chapters.text: Venetian merchants smuggled the body of St. Mark out of Alexandria in 828. The church built for it, consecrated in 1094, was modeled on a church in Constantinople. After 1204 it was covered in marble, columns, and mosaics looted from that city.
chapters.image: (Venice) St. Mark's Basilica, lunette - The body of St. Mark is received in Venice, ca. 1660 by Pietro Vecchia.jpg

chapters.heading: The first Gothic
chapters.text: Abbot Suger rebuilt the choir of Saint-Denis in the 1140s with pointed arches and walls of glass, and Gothic was born. Notre-Dame was begun in 1163. In April 2019 fire destroyed its roof and spire. It reopened in December 2024, rebuilt by carpenters and masons using medieval methods.
chapters.image: Basilica of Saint Denis, Saint Denis, France 02.jpg

chapters.heading: Built on a mosque
chapters.text: Seville’s chapter decided in 1401 to build a church so big that people would think them mad. It went up on the site of the Almohad mosque, and kept the mosque’s minaret as its bell tower, the Giralda. It is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world, and holds a tomb said to contain Columbus.
chapters.image: Plaza Virgen de los Reyes, Seville, Spain - Sep 2009.jpg

chapters.heading: Brunelleschi’s dome
chapters.text: Florence’s cathedral stood with a hole in its roof for decades because no one knew how to span it. Filippo Brunelleschi, a goldsmith, built the dome without a wooden frame, laying bricks in a herringbone pattern so each ring held itself up. It is still the largest brick dome ever built.
chapters.tip: You can climb between the two shells of the dome to the lantern. Book a time slot ahead.
chapters.image: Florence, Italy, Brunelleschi's Dome of Florence Cathedral.jpg

chapters.heading: Six centuries
chapters.text: Milan began its cathedral in 1386 in white Candoglia marble and kept going for nearly six centuries. Napoleon had the façade finished so he could be crowned there in 1805, and the last bronze door went in in 1965. In Milanese, an endless job is still called a fabbrica del Duomo.

chapters.heading: St. Peter’s
chapters.text: Pope Julius II had the old basilica pulled down in 1506. Bramante, Michelangelo, Maderno, and Bernini followed one another over 120 years, and the sale of indulgences to pay for it helped set off the Reformation. Bernini’s bronze canopy went up over the altar in 1634, and his colonnade was finished in 1667.
chapters.image: Basilica di San Pietro in Vaticano September 2015-1a.jpg

chapters.heading: Wren’s St. Paul’s
chapters.text: The Great Fire of 1666 ruined old St. Paul’s. Christopher Wren’s replacement was built from 1675 to 1710, and he lived to see it finished. On December 29, 1940, German bombs set the City around it on fire, and a photograph of its dome rising through the smoke became the image of the Blitz.
chapters.image: St Paul's Cathedra Millennium Bridge JBU04.jpg

chapters.heading: Gaudí’s basilica
chapters.text: The Sagrada Família was begun in 1882, and Antoni Gaudí took it over the next year. He spent the rest of his life on it and was killed by a tram in 1926 with less than a quarter built. Work has gone on ever since, paid for by visitors’ tickets.

chapters.heading: Two cathedrals
chapters.text: Giles Gilbert Scott was 22 when he won the competition for Liverpool’s Anglican cathedral. Building began in 1904 and finished in 1978, after his death. At the other end of Hope Street, Lutyens’s Catholic cathedral, meant to have a dome bigger than St. Peter’s, stopped at the crypt. Frederick Gibberd’s round concrete one went up on top in 1967.
chapters.image: Liverpool Metropolitan Cathedral at dusk (reduced grain), corrected perspective.jpg

image: Dome of Cattedrale di Santa Maria del Fiore (Florence).jpg

title: Bridges
intro: A bridge decides how a city grows, and holding one has often decided who holds the city.
The stops run from a Roman emperor’s bridge to one made by a robot.

chapters.heading: The emperor’s bridge
chapters.text: Hadrian built this bridge in 134 to reach his mausoleum, now the Castel Sant’Angelo. For centuries pilgrims crossed it to St. Peter’s, and criminals were executed at its end. Beatrice Cenci was beheaded there in 1599 for the murder of her abusive father. Bernini’s workshop added the ten angels around 1670.

chapters.place: London Bridge and Tower Bridge, London
chapters.heading: London’s bridges
chapters.text: For most of its history London had one bridge. Norse sagas say Olaf Haraldsson pulled the wooden one down in 1014. The stone bridge that followed carried houses and shops, and traitors’ heads on spikes. Watermen rowed everyone else across until a second central bridge opened at Westminster in 1750. Tower Bridge, with its lifting roadway, opened in 1894.

chapters.heading: The bridge they spared
chapters.text: The Ponte Vecchio was rebuilt after a flood in 1345 with shops along it. In 1565 Vasari built a private corridor across its roof so Cosimo I de’ Medici could walk from palace to palace unseen, and in 1593 the butchers below were replaced by goldsmiths. In August 1944 the retreating Germans blew up every other bridge in the city.
chapters.image: Ponte Vecchio from Ponte Santa Trinita Blue hour.jpg

chapters.heading: Charles Bridge
chapters.text: Charles IV laid the first stone in 1357, and for four centuries it was Prague’s only bridge over the Vltava. In 1393 the priest John of Nepomuk was thrown from it on the king’s orders. His statue, put up in 1683, was the first of the thirty Baroque saints that now line the parapets.
chapters.tip: Go before 8 in the morning, when it is almost empty.
chapters.image: Prague 07-2016 View from Petrinska Tower img2.jpg

chapters.heading: The Rialto
chapters.text: Wooden bridges at the Rialto kept burning or falling down, once under a crowd watching a wedding procession. The stone one was built from 1588 to 1591 by Antonio da Ponte, whose name means bridge. It was the only way across the Grand Canal on foot until 1854.

chapters.place: South Bridge and the Forth Bridge, Edinburgh
chapters.heading: Over valleys and firths
chapters.text: Edinburgh’s South Bridge, finished in 1788, carries a street over the Cowgate on a row of arches, and the vaults inside it became workshops, taverns, and slum rooms. A century later the red cantilever Forth Bridge, opened in 1890, carried the railway across the Firth of Forth west of the city.

chapters.heading: Joining Buda and Pest
chapters.text: Buda and Pest had no permanent bridge until Count István Széchenyi pushed for one. Its English designer, William Tierney Clark, and Scottish engineer, Adam Clark, finished the Chain Bridge in 1849. The Germans blew it up in January 1945, and it was rebuilt by 1949.
chapters.image: Széchenyi Chain Bridge in Budapest at night.jpg

chapters.heading: A bridge full of water
chapters.text: When the Manchester Ship Canal opened in 1894 to make the city a seaport, it had to cross the older Bridgewater Canal. The answer was a steel trough that holds the water of one canal and swings aside, full, to let ships pass on the other. It still works.

chapters.heading: Between two continents
chapters.text: The Bosphorus Bridge opened in 1973, the first to join the European and Asian sides of Istanbul. On the night of July 15, 2016, soldiers trying to overthrow the government blocked it with tanks, and civilians came out to face them. It has been called the 15 July Martyrs Bridge since.
chapters.image: Bosphorus Bridge(15 July Martyrs Bridge), Istanbul, Turkey (Ank Kumar) 12.jpg

chapters.heading: A printed bridge
chapters.text: Amsterdam has more than 1,500 bridges. In 2021 one of the newest was installed over a canal in the old center: a stainless-steel footbridge printed by robots, layer by layer, by the Dutch company MX3D. Sensors in it recorded how people used it.
chapters.image: World first 3D printed steel bridge in Amsterdam.jpg

image: Prague morning - View towards Charles Bridge - Flickr - A Peach.jpg

title: Markets
intro: A city’s markets show you what it eats, what it sells, and who lives there.

They also last. Some of the markets in this thread have traded on the same spot for hundreds of years. The stops run in order of age, from the market halls of ancient Rome to a quay in Marseille where fishermen still sell their catch every morning.

chapters.heading: Rome’s ancient shopping street
chapters.text: The oldest stop is in Rome, and it is nearly two thousand years old. Around the year 100 the emperor Trajan had a new forum built, a public square for the city’s business. Beside it his architect, Apollodorus of Damascus, cut into the Quirinal hill and built a curving complex of brick halls and vaulted rooms on several levels. It is usually called Trajan’s Markets. Some of the rooms were probably offices, so the name may flatter it. Even so, it is the best-preserved shopping street of the ancient world.

items: To see how it was put together, there is a short video about how Trajan’s Markets were built and what they held.

chapters.heading: A square laid out for trade
chapters.text: Long after Rome’s empire was gone, the towns of Europe traded in the open, on a market square. One of the biggest is in Kraków, in southern Poland. Mongol armies burned the city in 1241. In 1257 it was laid out again around a square of about four hectares, one of the largest in medieval Europe. The long building in the middle, the Cloth Hall, was its trading floor. The ground has risen since then, and the medieval market now lies about four meters below the paving. Archaeologists dug out its stalls and roads, and you can walk among them in a museum under the square. Just north of the old town, farmers still sell produce at Stary Kleparz, which has been a market since the 1300s.
chapters.image: Kraków Cloth Hall, Café Noworolski, 3 Main Market square, Old Town, Kraków, Poland.jpg

mediaNote.lead: There are three ways to explore Kraków’s markets further.
items: A podcast episode tells how the city grew rich on trade and survived the Mongols.
One short video goes down into the museum under the square.
Another visits the farmers’ stalls at Stary Kleparz.

chapters.heading: Four thousand shops under one roof
chapters.text: Two centuries later, another city put its market under a roof. In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed the Second, known as the Conqueror, took Constantinople, the city now called Istanbul. Soon afterward he built a domed warehouse where merchants could lock up their valuables. Streets of shops grew around it, and over time those streets were roofed in too. The result is the Grand Bazaar. It now holds about 4,000 shops on some sixty lanes.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here take you inside the bazaar.
items: A podcast episode tells its history, including its darker stories.
A short video walks through the lanes.

chapters.heading: When a tulip cost a house
chapters.text: Markets do not only sell things you can carry home. In the 1630s traders in the Dutch Republic, as the Netherlands was then called, bought and sold tulip bulbs that were still in the ground. In the winter of 1636 and 1637 the price of rare bulbs kept rising, until a single bulb could cost as much as a house on an Amsterdam canal. In February the prices collapsed. The story is often told as the first financial bubble. Historians now think the damage was smaller than the legend. Amsterdam still sells bulbs at the Bloemenmarkt, a flower market on the Singel canal, where traders have worked from boats since 1862.
chapters.image: Amsterdam - Singel - Bloemenmarkt - Flowermarket - View WNW I.jpg

items: If you want to understand the bubble, there is a short podcast episode in which an economist explains how the tulip trade worked.

chapters.heading: Madrid’s Sunday flea market
chapters.text: A different kind of market sells what people no longer want. In Madrid it happens every Sunday, in the streets that run downhill from La Latina, an old neighborhood in the center. The flea market there is called El Rastro, and it has been going since about 1740. It grew up in the tanners’ district, near the slaughterhouse. Rastro means trail, and the name is said to come from the blood left behind when carcasses were dragged down the hill. For food, Madrid has the Mercado de San Miguel, an iron-and-glass hall that opened nearby in 1916.

mediaNote.lead: Here are two things worth a look before a Sunday in Madrid.
items: A podcast episode recorded at El Rastro describes what is for sale and gives tips for a visit.
A short video picks out things to eat at the Mercado de San Miguel.

chapters.heading: Florence’s iron-and-glass food hall
chapters.text: Iron-and-glass halls like San Miguel were an invention of the 1800s. They let cities build big, bright buildings and move their food sellers indoors. Florence built its central market this way in 1874, in the San Lorenzo district. The architect was Giuseppe Mengoni, who also designed the Galleria, the glass-roofed shopping arcade in Milan. The ground floor still sells meat, cheese, and vegetables. It is also the place to try lampredotto, a sandwich made from the fourth stomach of a cow. Florentines line up for it.

items: If you are curious about that sandwich, there is a video about lampredotto, and the people who line up for it.

chapters.heading: The ragpickers’ market outside Paris
chapters.text: While Florence was moving its food sellers indoors, Paris was pushing its poorest traders out. In the 1880s the city’s ragpickers, people who made a living sorting through trash for things to sell, were moved outside the city walls. They set up just beyond the northern gate, at Saint-Ouen. The market became known as les puces, the fleas. It grew into one of the largest antiques markets in the world. Today it is a dozen separate markets with about 1,700 dealers.

items: To see what it looks like today, there is a short video that explores the stalls at Les Puces and stops for lunch.

chapters.heading: Budapest’s hall beside the Danube
chapters.text: In the 1890s Budapest built a market hall of its own, and built it big. The Great Market Hall opened in 1897 beside the Liberty Bridge, on the bank of the Danube. It is a long steel hall under a roof of colored tiles made by Zsolnay, a Hungarian ceramics firm. Barges once brought goods straight inside, through a tunnel from the river. The ground floor is still full of paprika, sausages, and pickles.

mediaNote.lead: Two videos here go further into the hall and its food.
items: One looks around the market hall.
The other tells the story of goulash, the paprika stew that became Hungary’s national dish.

chapters.heading: The Barras, built from barrows
chapters.text: Glasgow’s best-known market started with one woman and some handcarts. Maggie McIver rented out barrows to street traders in the East End of the city. In the 1920s she built a covered market for them on the Gallowgate, one of the main streets there. It was called the Barras, the local word for barrows. Her traders wanted somewhere to go in the evening. So in 1934 she built a dance hall above the market, the Barrowland Ballroom. It later became one of Britain’s best-loved rock venues.

mediaNote.lead: There are two ways to hear more about Maggie McIver’s market.
items: A video marks a hundred years of the Barras.
A podcast episode tells the story of the Barrowland Ballroom.

chapters.heading: Fish off the boat in Marseille
chapters.text: The last stop is the simplest market of all. Every morning, fishermen tie up at the Quai des Belges, the quay at the head of Marseille’s Old Port, and sell their catch straight off the boats. They have done it for generations. This is where bouillabaisse starts, the fish stew the city is known for. The American cook Julia Child lived in Marseille in the 1950s, and years later she made the stew on television. Trajan’s Markets are a ruin now. On this quay the oldest kind of market carries on: someone with something to sell, and a place to stand.
chapters.tip: Get there by 8; most of the fish is gone by mid-morning.

mediaNote.lead: Two things here follow the fish from the quay to the pot.
items: A podcast episode uses bouillabaisse to tell the story of who came to Marseille.
The other is the Julia Child episode, in which she makes the stew.

title: Parks and gardens
intro: Gardens began as private paradises for emperors and kings. Over time most of them were opened up, and cities began making parks for everyone.
The stops run from a painted Roman garden to a park in Istanbul that people protested to save.

chapters.heading: A painted garden
chapters.text: The empress Livia had an underground dining room at her villa north of Rome painted floor to ceiling as a garden, with fruit trees, flowers, and birds. The frescoes were cut from the walls and moved to the Palazzo Massimo museum, where the room has been rebuilt.

chapters.heading: A garden of medicines
chapters.text: The city founded the Hortus Botanicus in 1638 as a herb garden for doctors and apothecaries, during an outbreak of plague. Ships of the Dutch East India Company brought back plants from Asia, Africa, and the Americas, and some went on from here to plantations around the world.

chapters.heading: Le Nôtre’s Versailles
chapters.text: From 1661 André Le Nôtre laid out the gardens of Versailles for Louis XIV: terraces, clipped hedges, fountains, and a mile-long canal on which the king kept gondolas. The design was copied by every court in Europe. The Tuileries in central Paris were also his.

chapters.heading: Kew
chapters.text: Princess Augusta started a botanic garden at Kew in 1759. William Chambers built the ten-story Great Pagoda in 1762, and the iron-and-glass Palm House, finished in 1848, was built to hold tropical plants collected across the empire. Kew is still a research institution.
chapters.image: Kew Gardens Palm House, London - July 2009.jpg

chapters.heading: The last king’s park
chapters.text: Stanisław August Poniatowski, the last king of Poland, turned a bathhouse in a park south of Warsaw into a small palace standing in a lake, the Palace on the Isle. He lost his throne when Poland was partitioned in 1795. On summer Sundays there are Chopin concerts by the monument in the park.

chapters.heading: Skansen
chapters.text: Artur Hazelius worried that industry was wiping out rural Sweden, so he bought old farmhouses, churches, and workshops from around the country and rebuilt them on a hill on Djurgården. Skansen opened in 1891, the world’s first open-air museum.

chapters.heading: Allotments
chapters.text: Copenhagen’s kolonihaver are allotment gardens, each with a small house, rented by city dwellers. Vennelyst on Amager was founded in 1892. They were meant to give working families fresh vegetables, and waiting lists for them now run to years.

chapters.heading: Vigeland
chapters.text: In 1921 the sculptor Gustav Vigeland agreed to give Oslo all his future work in return for a studio. He spent the rest of his life filling Frogner Park with more than 200 granite and bronze figures, crowned by a granite column of 121 bodies.
chapters.image: Vigeland Sculpture Park - Granite sculptures on the staircase, Oslo, Norway.jpg

chapters.heading: Needle Park
chapters.text: From 1987 the Platzspitz, a riverside park behind the Swiss National Museum, was where Zurich’s police let heroin users gather. Thousands came from across Europe. The park was closed in 1992, and Switzerland moved to prescribing heroin under medical supervision. The park has been open again since 1993.

chapters.heading: Gezi Park
chapters.text: In May 2013 a few dozen people camped in Gezi Park, beside Taksim Square, to stop its trees being cut down for a shopping center. The police burned their tents, and within days there were protests in cities across Turkey. The park is still there.
chapters.image: İstanbul - Taksim Gezi Parkı - Mart 2013 - r7.JPG

image: Versailles view from the Parterre d'eau.jpg

title: The coffeehouse
intro: Coffee came to Europe from the Ottoman Empire, and the coffeehouse came with it: a public room where anyone who could pay for a cup could sit, read, and argue. Writers worked in them, spies met in them, and governments tried more than once to shut them down.
This thread starts in Istanbul and ends in Lisbon. Almost every stop is a café you can still sit in.

chapters.heading: Where it started
chapters.text: Coffee came from Yemen, across the Red Sea from Arabia, and in the 1550s it reached Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire. The city’s first coffeehouses opened in Tahtakale, the market district by the Golden Horn. They caught on fast. Men met there to talk, play games, and listen to storytellers, and the authorities did not like it. Sultans and religious leaders tried more than once to close them as places of gossip and rebellion, but the coffeehouses always came back. Three hundred years later, European and Levantine families built a different kind of café life across the water, in the district of Pera, along the street now called İstiklal Avenue.
chapters.tip: Turkish coffee is served with its grounds. Let them settle, and stop drinking before you reach them.

mediaNote.lead: Two podcast episodes cover each side of the story.
items: A comedy history podcast about the Ottoman court covers coffeehouse culture, along with law codes and festivals.
An episode of the Ottoman History Podcast follows the Vallaury family, who ran cafés on the main street of Pera.

chapters.heading: A seat for the afternoon
chapters.text: From Istanbul, coffee spread west to Venice, London, and Paris. But the city that made the coffeehouse its own was Vienna, which the Ottoman army besieged in 1683. Its first licensed coffeehouse opened two years later. By 1900 there were hundreds, and the coffeehouse had become the city’s shared living room, warmer and more comfortable than many people’s homes. For the price of one cup you could stay all afternoon, read the newspapers, and write letters. Café Central, opened in 1876 in a grand former bank on Herrengasse, drew writers, chess players, and political exiles. Leon Trotsky, the Russian revolutionary, played chess there before the First World War. In 2011 Vienna’s coffeehouse culture was listed as intangible heritage by Austria’s commission for UNESCO.
chapters.tip: One coffee buys a seat for as long as you like. It comes with a glass of water, and you can ask for the newspapers.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to understand the Viennese café.
items: A podcast episode about the coffee trade explores the grand cafés where writers lingered for hours.
A short video shows what you get for the price of one coffee, from the marble tables to the newspapers.
And Stefan Zweig’s memoir The World of Yesterday remembers the café-going Vienna he grew up in, before the wars ended it.

chapters.place: Grand Café, Karl Johans gate, Oslo
chapters.heading: Ibsen’s lunch
chapters.text: In the late 1800s, the Viennese idea of the café spread north and east. In Kristiania, as Oslo was then called, the Grand Café on Karl Johans gate, the main street, became the meeting place of writers and artists. Its most famous regular was Henrik Ibsen, the playwright of A Doll’s House and Hedda Gabler. He came home in 1891 after nearly thirty years abroad. Each day he walked to the Grand Café at the same time and sat at the same table. People said you could set your watch by him, and visitors came to see him arrive. A large mural inside, painted in the 1920s, shows him among the city’s writers and artists.

items: If you want to know the man behind the routine, there is a biography of Ibsen, the prickly playwright who changed modern theater.

chapters.heading: Six hundred coffeehouses
chapters.text: Budapest took to coffeehouses with even more enthusiasm. Around 1900 it was one of the fastest-growing cities in Europe, and it had about six hundred cafés. Writers had their regular tables, magazines were edited from them, and some cafés never closed at all. Many were lost in the Second World War, and more under communism, when they were seen as bourgeois. Gerbeaud, a confectioner’s café that has stood on Vörösmarty Square since 1870, is one of the grand ones that survived.

mediaNote.lead: Two books bring that world back.
items: John Lukacs’s Budapest 1900 is a portrait of the city at its peak, full of coffeehouses, poets, and money.
In Between the Woods and the Water, Patrick Leigh Fermor, who walked across Europe at nineteen, falls in with Budapest’s café society in 1934.

chapters.heading: Art Nouveau rooms
chapters.text: Prague built its grand cafés in the same years, when the city was rich and growing fast. In the 1900s and 1910s, the writer Franz Kafka met his friends at the Café Louvre on Národní, the avenue that runs down to the river. Café Slavia, across the street from the National Theatre, was where actors and writers went after the show. Under communism it became a meeting place for dissidents, among them Václav Havel, the playwright who became president after the revolution of 1989. The café inside the Municipal House, an Art Nouveau concert hall opened in 1912, still has its original interior.
chapters.tip: The café inside the Municipal House keeps its original 1912 interior.

mediaNote.lead: Two walking tours cover this well.
items: A tour of the New Town takes in Art Nouveau buildings and elegant cafés, and ends on the avenue where the Velvet Revolution began.
Another follows Kafka through the old town, with readings from his work, and ends near a café he went to.

chapters.heading: Spies on Terazije
chapters.text: Farther south, Belgrade’s best-known café opened in 1908 on the ground floor of the Hotel Moskva, a grand building on Terazije, the city’s main square. Through two world wars and the Cold War, it was where diplomats, journalists, and agents watched each other over coffee. Yugoslavia belonged to neither the Soviet bloc nor the West, so both sides worked in Belgrade, and the café was one of their favorite places to meet. It still serves its own cake, the Moskva šnit, made with pineapple, cherries, and almonds.
chapters.image: Hotel Moskva and the fountain in Belgrade.jpg

items: For a spy’s view of it, there is a podcast episode in which a former CIA officer describes meeting a Yugoslav source in Belgrade’s cafés.

chapters.heading: The poets’ table
chapters.text: Between the two world wars, Warsaw had its own poets’ café. Mała Ziemiańska, on Mazowiecka Street, opened in 1918, the year Poland became independent again. Its upstairs room belonged to the Skamander group, young poets such as Julian Tuwim and Antoni Słonimski, who wrote about ordinary city life in everyday language. The other tables went to painters, actors, and journalists. In 1939 Germany invaded Poland, and in 1944, after the Warsaw Uprising, the German army destroyed most of the city center. The café was never rebuilt.

items: To see where it stood, there is a video from POLIN, the museum of Polish Jewish history, about the café and the poets who held court there.

chapters.heading: The existentialists’ café
chapters.text: Paris had cafés long before Vienna’s golden age. The Procope, which opened in 1686, is often called the oldest in the city. But it was in the 1940s that the Paris café became a symbol of intellectual life. During the German occupation, the philosophers Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir worked most days at the Café de Flore, on Boulevard Saint-Germain. One reason was that the café was heated and their rooms were not. After the war their ideas, known as existentialism, became famous around the world, and so did the cafés of Saint-Germain-des-Prés where they wrote.
chapters.tip: Coffee costs less standing at the counter than at a table, and more on the terrace.
chapters.image: Café de Flore, 172 boulevard Saint-Germain, Paris 6e.jpg

mediaNote.lead: Here are two ways into Paris café life.
items: Sarah Bakewell’s At the Existentialist Café tells the story of Sartre, Beauvoir, and their friends, and makes their ideas easy to follow.
A very short video looks at the café life of the Latin Quarter, next door to Saint-Germain.

chapters.heading: Pessoa’s table
chapters.text: The thread ends in Lisbon, where coffee has a special link to Brazil, Portugal’s former colony and one of the world’s largest coffee growers. A Brasileira opened in the Chiado district in 1905 to sell Brazilian coffee, and it gave a free cup to everyone who bought a bag of beans. It became a meeting place for writers and artists. Its best-known customer was Fernando Pessoa, a poet who wrote under dozens of invented names. A bronze statue of him sits at a table outside. His other favorite, Martinho da Arcada, on the great riverside square called the Praça do Comércio, has been open since 1782.
chapters.tip: In Lisbon an espresso is “uma bica.”

mediaNote.lead: If you want to linger in Pessoa’s Lisbon, here are three places to start.
items: The Book of Disquiet, his strange, fragmentary diary of a Lisbon bookkeeper, is best read in short pieces.
A one-minute video at Martinho da Arcada explains five ways to order coffee like a local.
And a short photography walk starts at a café where poets and painters once met, and heads down to the river.

title: Beer
intro: Northern Europe drank beer before it drank water safely, and its breweries grew into some of its biggest businesses. Several of them built museums, palaces, and art collections with the money.
Beer halls have also been the backdrop to some darker history.

chapters.heading: U Fleků
chapters.text: U Fleků has brewed its dark lager in Prague’s New Town since at least 1499. Czechs drink more beer per person than anyone, and the city’s pubs are where the good soldier Švejk plots his way through the First World War.

chapters.heading: Purity and Oktoberfest
chapters.text: Bavaria’s 1516 purity law said beer could be made only from barley, hops, and water. The dukes opened the Hofbräuhaus as their court brewery in 1589. Oktoberfest started in 1810 as a horse race for a royal wedding.

chapters.heading: Guinness
chapters.text: In 1759 Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on a brewery at St. James’s Gate. His dark porter became Ireland’s best-known export, and the brewery is still there.

chapters.heading: The beer flood
chapters.text: In October 1814 a huge vat burst at the Meux brewery off Tottenham Court Road, and over a million liters of porter swept through the slums behind it. Eight people died.

chapters.heading: Beer halls and the Nazis
chapters.text: Hitler announced the Nazi party’s program in the Hofbräuhaus in 1920, and in 1923 he fired a shot into the ceiling of the Bürgerbräukeller to start a failed coup. In 1939 a carpenter, Georg Elser, hid a bomb in a pillar there that missed Hitler by thirteen minutes.

chapters.heading: Carlsberg
chapters.text: J.C. Jacobsen founded Carlsberg in 1847. In 1883 its laboratory isolated a pure lager yeast and gave it away, and most lager in the world now descends from it. His son Carl spent the profits on art and founded the Ny Carlsberg Glyptotek. Today small brewpubs have spread across the city.

title: Wine
intro: Europe has made wine for nearly three thousand years, and the trade in it has shaped cities, treaties, and tastes.

This thread follows wine from the Greek settlers who planted the first vines in France to a community vineyard on the edge of London. Along the way it stops at a sherry town in Spain, a wine tavern in Vienna, and a blind tasting in Paris that changed the business.

chapters.heading: Greeks plant the first vines
chapters.text: The story begins at the harbor that is now Marseille. Around 600 BC, Greek settlers from Phocaea, a city on the coast of what is now Turkey, founded a trading town there and called it Massalia. They brought vines and olive trees with them, and they planted the first vineyards in Gaul, the land that would become France. From the harbor, wine traveled up the river Rhône to peoples in the north who had never made it.

items: To hear more about the city’s Greek beginnings, there is a podcast episode about the settlers who founded it.

chapters.heading: Harvest scenes on a Christian tomb
chapters.text: The Romans spread vines across their empire, and wine was part of daily life for anyone who could afford it. When the empire became Christian, wine did not lose its place, because it was central to the Mass. You can see the old and new meet in a round building on the edge of Rome, built around 350 as a tomb for Constantina, a daughter of the emperor Constantine. Its ceiling mosaics show small winged figures picking grapes, carting them in, and treading them, the same scenes that had decorated pagan villas.

items: For a closer look at the mosaics, there is a short video about the building and the grape harvest on its ceiling.

chapters.place: Jerez de la Frontera, near Seville
chapters.heading: Sherry goes around the world
chapters.text: In the 1500s, wine from southern Spain sailed further than any wine before it. It came from Jerez, a town south of Seville that the Moors had called Sherish. English merchants turned that name into “sherry.” When Ferdinand Magellan set out in 1519 on the voyage that first sailed around the world, his ships are said to have carried more sherry than weapons. In England it became a fashion. Falstaff, the drinking knight in Shakespeare’s plays, gives a whole speech in praise of it.

mediaNote.lead: There are two good places to start with sherry.
items: A podcast episode tells how the town’s name became sherry.
In another, a sherry enthusiast explains the bodegas, the wineries where it ages, from La Venencia, an old sherry bar in Madrid.

chapters.image: Bodega Gonzalez- Byas Jerez de la Frontera.JPG

chapters.heading: The English and port
chapters.text: The English never made much wine, but they shaped how it was made elsewhere. When wars with France cut off French wine, English merchants turned to Portugal. A treaty in 1703 lowered the tax on Portuguese wine, and English and Scottish firms set up in Porto, at the mouth of the Douro river. To keep the wine sound on the voyage north, they added brandy to it, and port was born. Several of the big port houses still have British names.

items: To hear how that family trade continues, there is a podcast episode with the son of a port maker who now runs a Portuguese restaurant in London.

chapters.image: Boats of Port Wine in Vila Nova de Gaia, Porto in the background - panoramio.jpg

chapters.heading: A wine city with its own taverns
chapters.text: Vienna is one of the few capitals that still grows wine inside its city limits, on the hills to the north and west. In 1784 the emperor Joseph II allowed growers to sell their own wine, and simple food to go with it, without a license. That gave rise to the Heuriger, a wine tavern where you drink the new vintage. A grower who has wine to sell hangs a bundle of pine branches over the door, and villages like Grinzing, on the city’s edge, are full of them.

mediaNote.lead: Two pieces bring you to the table.
items: A short video visits the winemakers of Grinzing.
A food walk through the old center includes a glass of Viennese wine.

chapters.place: Site of Les Caves de la Madeleine, Paris
chapters.heading: The tasting that upset France
chapters.text: For two centuries, everyone agreed that the best wine came from France. Then, in May 1976, Steven Spurrier, an English wine merchant with a shop in Paris, held a blind tasting. French experts tasted top French wines alongside new ones from California, without knowing which was which. A Californian wine won in both the red and the white categories. A single journalist was there to report it, and the result changed what the world thought wine from outside Europe could be.

items: For the story from someone who was there, there is a short podcast episode about the tasting.

chapters.heading: A small glass in the shade
chapters.text: Most wine in Europe is still drunk in a simple way. In Venice, people stop at a bàcaro, a small wine bar, for an ombra, a small glass of house wine, and a few cicchetti, the snacks on the counter. Ombra means shade. One story says it comes from the wine sellers who once moved their stalls around St. Mark’s Square to stay in the shadow of the bell tower. The oldest bàcari are near the Rialto market, and some claim to have been pouring for five hundred years.

mediaNote.lead: Here are three ways to find the right bar.
items: A short video tours the bars around the Rialto.
A drinks writer talks about her guide to drinking in Venice.
A walking tour stops at five of the old bars.

chapters.heading: Vines in north London
chapters.text: The thread ends where you might least expect wine. England was long too cold and damp for good grapes. As summers have warmed, vineyards have spread across the south of the country, and English sparkling wine now wins prizes. On the northern edge of London, in Enfield, volunteers tend Forty Hall Vineyard, the only commercial vineyard in the city, and make wine from its grapes.

items: To meet the people who work it, there is a short video about the vineyard and its volunteers.

title: Olympic cities
intro: The modern Olympics began in Athens in 1896, and European cities have used them since to rebuild, to show off, and once to make propaganda. Most of the stadiums are still in use.
The stops run in date order.

chapters.heading: The first modern Games
chapters.text: Pierre de Coubertin’s revived Olympics opened in 1896 in Athens’ ancient stadium, rebuilt in white marble. The Greek water carrier Spyridon Louis won the first marathon.

chapters.heading: Hitler’s Games
chapters.text: The Nazis used the 1936 Games to show the world a confident Germany. Jesse Owens, a Black American, won four gold medals in their new stadium.

chapters.heading: The skater from Oslo
chapters.text: Sonja Henie from Oslo won figure-skating gold at three Winter Olympics in a row, from 1928 to 1936, then became a Hollywood star. Oslo hosted the Winter Games in 1952.
chapters.image: Holmenkollbakken - no-nb digifoto 20150625 00168 NB MIT FNR 11656 B.jpg

chapters.heading: Helsinki 1952
chapters.text: Helsinki finally hosted the Games in 1952, after the 1940 Olympics were canceled by the war. The Soviet Union competed for the first time, and the Czech runner Emil Zátopek won the 5,000 meters, the 10,000 meters, and the marathon in eight days.

chapters.heading: The cheerful Games
chapters.text: West Germany wanted 1972 to be the opposite of 1936: pastel colors, Otl Aicher’s pictograms, a tent-like stadium roof. On September 5, Palestinian gunmen took Israeli athletes hostage in the Olympic village, and eleven of them were killed.

chapters.heading: The city rebuilt
chapters.text: Barcelona used the 1992 Games to open itself to the sea, replacing old industrial waterfront with beaches and a new Olympic village. It is still the model other host cities point to.
chapters.image: Aerial view of Somorrostro Beach and Port Olympic in Barcelona, Spain (51227006624).jpg

chapters.heading: East London
chapters.text: London put its 2012 Games in Stratford, in the East End, on old industrial land. Zaha Hadid’s aquatics center is now a public pool.

title: Football cities
intro: In most of Europe a football club is more than a team. It can stand for a religion in Glasgow, a nation in Barcelona, a country that no longer exists in Belgrade. Grounds are places of pilgrimage and, more than once, of disaster.
Each stop is a stadium, with the story of what it means to the city.

chapters.heading: The Old Firm
chapters.text: Celtic was founded in 1887 by an Irish Marist brother to raise money for the poor of Glasgow’s East End, and became the club of the city’s Irish Catholics. Rangers became the club of its Protestants. In 1967 Celtic were the first British side to win the European Cup. In 1971, 66 people died on a stairway at Ibrox after a New Year derby.

chapters.heading: The Kop
chapters.text: Bill Shankly arrived in 1959 and built Liverpool into a winning club. The Kop, the huge standing terrace, adopted “You’ll Never Walk Alone” in 1963. In 1989, 97 Liverpool fans died in a crush at Hillsborough in Sheffield. It took 27 years and a second inquest to establish that they had been unlawfully killed.
chapters.image: The Kop at Anfield Stadium, Liverpool - geograph.org.uk - 5885064.jpg

chapters.heading: After Munich
chapters.text: In February 1958 the plane carrying Manchester United home from a European tie crashed on take-off after refueling in Munich. Twenty-three people died, eight of them players. Matt Busby rebuilt the team, which won the European Cup ten years later.

chapters.heading: More than a club
chapters.text: Under Franco, when Catalan was restricted, Barça’s ground was one of the few places tens of thousands of people could speak and shout it together. “Més que un club,” more than a club, is painted in the seats. The stadium is being rebuilt while the team plays on.

chapters.heading: The other side of El Clásico
chapters.text: Real Madrid won the first five European Cups and became, for many Catalans, the club of the regime. The Bernabéu, in the middle of the city, has just been rebuilt with a steel skin and a roof that closes.

chapters.heading: A city’s one club
chapters.text: Marseille has one big club, and the whole city follows it. In 1993 Olympique de Marseille became the first French side to win the Champions League. Its ultras groups run the two curves of the Vélodrome.

chapters.heading: Two clubs, one stadium
chapters.text: Inter was founded in 1908 by members who left AC Milan because they wanted to sign foreign players. The two clubs have shared San Siro since 1947. Under Helenio Herrera in the 1960s, Inter won two European Cups with a defensive style the world learned to call catenaccio.

chapters.place: FC Bayern Museum, Allianz Arena, Munich
chapters.heading: The Jewish president
chapters.text: Kurt Landauer was Bayern’s president when it won its first German title in 1932. The Nazis forced him out the next year, and he survived the war in exile in Switzerland. He came back and was president again after the war. The club now honors him openly.

chapters.place: Red Star and Partizan stadiums, Belgrade
chapters.heading: The Eternal Derby
chapters.text: Red Star and Partizan were both founded in 1945, and their grounds are a short walk apart. In May 1991 Red Star won the European Cup in Bari, on penalties, with players from across Yugoslavia. Within weeks the country began to break up, and the team with it.
